questions.stem: A company sells 60,000 calculators for $480,000. Variable costs are $252,000 and fixed costs are $180,000. What is the contribution margin ratio?
questions.solution:
1. Contribution margin = 480,000 − 252,000 = $228,000
  2. CM ratio = 228,000 / 480,000 = 47.5%

Per-unit route gives the same answer: price $8.00, VC $4.20, CM $3.80, and 3.80 / 8.00 = 47.5%.

Trap: 52.5% is the variable cost ratio. CM ratio + VC ratio = 100%.

questions.stem: Same company: price $8.00 per unit, variable cost $4.20 per unit, fixed costs $180,000. How many units must it sell to break even? (Round up to whole units.)
questions.solution:
1. CM per unit = 8.00 − 4.20 = $3.80
  2. Home equation: 8.00x − 4.20x − 180,000 = 0
  3. 3.80x = 180,000
  4. x = 47,368.42, round up to 47,369 units

You cannot sell a partial calculator, so unit break-even rounds up.

questions.stem: Same company. What is break-even in SALES DOLLARS?
questions.solution:
Dividing fixed cost by a percentage gives a dollar answer.

RouteCalculationResult
Ratio180,000 / 0.475$378,947
Percent formx − 0.525x − 180,000 = 0$378,947
Units × price47,368.42 × 8.00$378,947

Trap: when the answer is revenue dollars, X is revenue and the variable term is 0.525X. It is not $8 × volume.

questions.stem: Same company (price $8.00, VC $4.20, fixed $180,000). How many units are needed to earn operating income of $120,000?
questions.solution:
1. Put the target on the right side instead of zero: 8.00x − 4.20x − 180,000 = 120,000
  2. 3.80x = 300,000
  3. x = 78,947.37, round up to 78,948 units

Shortcut: (FC + target) / CM per unit = 300,000 / 3.80.

questions.stem: In the home equation, how is fixed cost handled?
choices: Divided by units to get fixed cost per unit
Subtracted from the variable cost rate
questions.solution:
Left alone in full. Fixed cost per unit is a "spready" number: it changes with volume, which is the one thing fixed cost is not supposed to do. There is no step in the home equation where you unitize fixed cost.

This also appears in multi-product CVP: "$210,000 total fixed cost left alone. Don't unitize."

questions.stem: Tom Flannery's father-in-law will invest $500,000 if the restaurant earns pre-tax profit of at least 20% of sales. Fixed expenses are $24,000 per year and variable expenses run about 40% of sales. What annual sales level meets the 20% target?
questions.solution:
1. Let x = sales dollars. The target is on both sides, and that is fine.
  2. x − 0.4x − 24,000 = 0.2x
  3. 0.6x − 24,000 = 0.2x
  4. 0.4x = 24,000
  5. x = $60,000

A target stated as a percent of sales puts X on both sides. Collect terms.

questions.stem: On a break-even chart, which line starts at the origin (zero)?
questions.solution:
LineStarts at
Revenuezero (origin)
Total costthe fixed cost level (y-intercept)
Fixed costflat, at its own level

They cross at break-even, where operating income = 0.

Trap: a line starting at the y-intercept is total cost, not variable cost. A variable-cost line starts at zero.

questions.stem: Why do accountants' straight-line 'variable' and 'fixed' labels work at all, given that economists object to them?
choices: Because costs are genuinely linear at all activity levels
Because they hold inside the relevant range
Because GAAP requires linear cost functions
Because regression forces a straight line
questions.solution: The relevant range is the limited band of activity over which the cost relationships are assumed constant. Inside it, the linear simplification is good enough to decide with. Push volume far outside the observed data and the labels stop holding.

questions.stem: Total contribution margin is $228,000 and operating income is $48,000. What is the degree of operating leverage?
questions.solution:
1. DOL = total CM dollars / operating income
  2. 228,000 / 48,000 = 4.75

Trap: DOL uses total contribution margin in dollars, never the CM ratio and never a percentage.

questions.stem: DOL is 4.75. Sales rise 20%. By how much does operating income change?
questions.solution:
1. % change in operating income = DOL × % change in sales
  2. 4.75 × 20% = +95%

Check it longhand:

StepAmount
CM grows 20%: 228,000 × 1.20$273,600
Less fixed cost (unchanged)(180,000)
New operating income$93,600
Change: (93,600 − 48,000) / 48,000+95%

questions.stem: Same firm, DOL 4.75. Sales FALL 20%. What happens to operating income?
questions.solution: Operating income falls 95%. Leverage is symmetric: the same multiplier works in both directions. "Leverage giveth and leverage taketh away."

questions.stem: Why is DOL a poor stand-alone measure of a firm's cost structure?
choices: It conflates fixed-cost intensity with proximity to break-even
It can only be computed after year-end
It requires a regression to estimate
questions.solution:
DOL mixes two unrelated drivers:

Driver of a high DOLWhat it tells you
Heavy fixed-cost intensitygenuine structural leverage
Sitting close to break-evena small denominator, nothing about structure

DOL is largest near break-even and shrinks as you move away, with cost structure held completely constant. So DOL alone is not interpretable; its value is the sensitivity statement it produces.

questions.stem: Firm A has VC of $4.20/unit and fixed cost of $180,000. Firm B has VC of $1.20/unit and fixed cost of $322,100. Both sell at $8.00 and both break even at 47,369 units. What distinguishes them?
choices: Nothing - identical break-even means identical risk
B loses more below break-even and earns more above it
questions.solution:
Identical break-even, completely different risk. B is the high-leverage structure.

  • Raising fixed cost lifts the total-cost line's intercept and flattens its slope.
  • Both the loss wedge below break-even and the profit wedge above it get bigger.

Operating leverage is the fixed-to-variable mix. Do not confuse it with financial leverage, which is debt versus equity.

questions.stem: PVC company: current volume 60,000 units, price $8.00, VC $4.20 per unit, fixed cost $180,000. What is the margin of safety in UNITS?
questions.solution:
1. CM per unit = 8.00 − 4.20 = $3.80
  2. Break-even units = 180,000 / 3.80 = 47,369
  3. MoS units = 60,000 − 47,369 = 12,631 units

Margin of safety is just one subtraction: what you sell minus what you need to sell.

questions.stem: Same PVC company. The question is: 'How far can sales decline before we reach break-even?' Which calculation answers it?
questions.solution:
Divide margin of safety by current sales: 12,631 / 60,000 = 21.05%.

Divide MoS byQuestion answered
Break-evenHow far above break-even are we?
Current salesHow far can sales decline before break-even?

Same numerator both times. Only the denominator changes. "Might be nice if these had different names, but they don't."

The professor said he would ask one of these two on the exam.

questions.stem: Same PVC company. The question is: 'How far ABOVE break-even are we?' What is the answer?
questions.solution:
Divide margin of safety by break-even: 12,631 / 47,369 = 26.7%.

Read the question wording carefully. "Above break-even" puts break-even in the denominator; "can decline" puts current sales there.

questions.stem: Same PVC company (MoS of 12,631 units, price $8.00). What is the margin of safety in sales DOLLARS?
questions.solution:
1. MoS dollars = MoS units × price = 12,631.58 × 8.00 = $101,053

Equivalently: current revenue $480,000 − break-even revenue $378,947 = $101,053.

Keep the unrounded 12,631.58. The rounded 12,631 × 8 is $101,048, five dollars short.

The dollar value of MoS is the same regardless of which percentage version you later compute.

questions.stem: A firm has HIGH structural operating leverage and a LOW margin of safety. Which description and examples match?
choices: Powerful but risky - data centers, software platforms
Precarious leverage - airlines, hotels, auto manufacturers
Fragile but flexible - restaurants, local retailers
The sweet spot - insurance agencies, asset-light service firms
questions.solution:
LeverageMoSLabelExamples

HighHighPowerful but riskydata centers, software platforms, streaming post-scale
LowLowFragile but flexiblerestaurants, local retailers, freelance operators

Leverage is about sensitivity of income to volume. Margin of safety is about distance from break-even. The professor warns that slotting industries into cells is "always a little dangerous."

questions.stem: A company targets after-tax net income of $500,000. Its tax rate is 30%. What operating income must it earn?
questions.solution:
1. Operating income in the home equation is a pre-tax number, so gross the target up.
  2. Operating income target = after-tax NI / (1 − tax rate)
  3. 500,000 / (1 − 0.30) = 500,000 / 0.70 = $714,286

This is as far as the course goes with taxes.

questions.stem: Investors want a 25% return on equity. Equity is $300,000 and the tax rate is 30%. What operating income is required?
questions.solution:
1. Return target × base: 0.25 × 300,000 = $75,000. This is an after-tax number.
  2. Gross up: 75,000 / (1 − 0.30) = $107,143

Trap: $75,000 is the most common wrong answer. A return target is after tax; you must gross it up before it goes on the right side of the home equation.

questions.stem: Video game problem. Volume 25,000 units, variable cost $40 per unit, fixed cost $120,000, equity $300,000, target ROE 30%, tax rate 40%. What SELLING PRICE is required? (Enter dollars per unit.)
questions.solution:
The unknown here is price, not volume. Identify X first.

StepCalculationResult
1. After-tax target0.30 × 300,000$90,000
2. Gross up for taxes90,000 / (1 − 0.40)$150,000
3. Home equation25,000P − (40 × 25,000) − 120,000 = 150,000
4. Collect25,000P = 150,000 + 120,000 + 1,000,000$1,270,000
5. Solve1,270,000 / 25,000$50.80

The $120,000 of fixed cost "including depreciation and interest" is a throwaway detail: it is still just fixed cost.

questions.stem: Calculators sell at $8.00 with VC of $4.20. Abacuses sell at $4.00 with VC of $2.80. The volume mix is 3 calculators to 1 abacus. What is the contribution margin per BASKET?
questions.solution:
StepCalculationResult
Basket revenue3 × 8.00 + 1 × 4.00$28.00
Basket variable cost3 × 4.20 + 1 × 2.80$15.40
Basket CM28.00 − 15.40$12.60

Equivalently: 3 × $3.80 + 1 × $1.20 = $12.60.

In class the professor said "$12" out loud, but his own break-even of 16,666.67 baskets only works with $12.60 (210,000 / 12.60).

questions.stem: Fixed costs are $210,000 and basket CM is $12.60 (3 calculators to 1 abacus). How many of each product does the firm sell at break-even?
questions.solution:
1. Break-even baskets = 210,000 / 12.60 = 16,666.67 : do not round this
  2. Calculators = 16,666.67 × 3 = 50,000
  3. Abacuses = 16,666.67 × 1 = 16,666.67, round up to 16,667

Why not round the baskets? "Baskets are not a thing." They exist only as a mathematical tool. Rounding is legitimate only once you are back in real units, and then you round up.

His slide uses a 6 : 2 basket, not 3 : 1. Both describe the same mix. With a 6 : 2 basket the basket contribution margin is $25.20 and break-even is $210,000 / $25.20 = 8,333.33 baskets, each holding 6 calculators and 2 abacuses. With a 3 : 1 basket it is $12.60 and 16,666.67 baskets of 3 and 1. Unpack either and you get the same product volumes, because 8,333.33 × 6 = 16,666.67 × 3. Reduce the mix or do not; the unpacked answer is unchanged.

questions.stem: Calculators: 60,000 units, $480,000 revenue, $252,000 variable cost. Abacuses: 20,000 units, $80,000 revenue, $56,000 variable cost. Fixed cost $210,000. Using the weighted-average method, what is break-even in TOTAL units?

WA price560,000 / 80,000$7.00
WA variable cost308,000 / 80,000$3.85
WA CM per unit7.00 − 3.85$3.15
Break-even total units210,000 / 3.1566,667

Nobody charges $7.00 and nobody charges $3.85. They are weighted averages, and that is fine.

Split by the volume mix: 75% → 50,000 calculators, 25% → 16,667 abacuses. Same as the basket answer.

questions.solution:

questions.stem: Combined break-even revenue is $466,666.67. Calculators generated $480,000 of the $560,000 total revenue; the volume mix is 3 to 1. What is CALCULATOR revenue at break-even?
questions.solution:
Split a revenue answer by the revenue mix, not the volume mix.

  1. 466,666.67 × 85.71% = $400,000

Trap: $350,000 is what you get by wrongly applying the 75% volume mix. "That's the volume mix. The revenue mix is different."

questions.stem: A multi-product question asks for break-even REVENUE by product. Which approach fits?
choices: Basket method, then multiply baskets by price
Weighted-average units, then split by volume mix
Revenue approach (FC / CM ratio), then split by revenue mix
Any of them - the split ratio does not matter
questions.solution:
Question asks forUse
Units, by productBasket, or weighted average then split by volume mix
Total revenue, or revenue by productRevenue approach, then split by revenue mix

All three methods agree on the underlying answer, but the split ratio is method-specific. Pick the approach by reading what is asked.

questions.stem: Goldman Company: total contribution margin $1.5 million on 200,000 units, fixed costs $1.2 million, sales mix 3 standard to 1 deluxe. What is break-even in total units?
questions.solution:
1. WA CM per unit = 1,500,000 / 200,000 = $7.50
  2. Break-even total units = 1,200,000 / 7.50 = 160,000
  3. Standard (75%) = 120,000; Deluxe (25%) = 40,000

Do not recompute per-unit data the problem already hands you.

Unresolved: two rounding orders, both his. The CVP Part 2 handout rounds each product up from the unrounded basket count, giving 181,819 total units. Homework 9-36 instead rounds the total up first and then applies the mix percentages to that rounded total, giving 181,820. One unit apart. Both appear in his own materials and neither is marked wrong.

What to do on the exam. Unpack first, then round each product up, which is the handout's order and the one his lecture follows. If a multiple-choice option sits one unit away from your answer, the other order is why; pick the nearer option and move on. On a typed answer, show the unrounded basket count so the method is visible.

questions.stem: What assumption do all three multi-product CVP methods require?
choices: The sales mix is known and constant
All products have the same contribution margin
questions.solution:
The sales mix is known and constant. State it if asked, and then immediately ask the follow-up question: how do these numbers flex if the mix changes?

Build sensitivity cells. Then ask whether the products are complements (mix moves together) or substitutes (mix moves in opposite directions), because that governs how the mix is likely to shift.

questions.stem: Regression of total cost on boats produced gives: intercept $49,701.29, slope $687.43. What do these two numbers represent?
choices: Intercept = variable rate; slope = fixed cost
Intercept = fixed cost; slope = variable cost rate
questions.solution:
The fitted line is Total cost = $49,701.29 + $687.43 per boat.

OutputMeans
Y-interceptfixed cost
Slopevariable cost rate

Same structure as high-low: y = mx + b.

questions.stem: The intercept's P value is 0.0974. What do you conclude?
choices: You cannot reject the null that fixed cost is zero
Fixed cost is statistically significant at 0.05
questions.solution:
1. Start from the null hypothesis: the relationship is zero.
  2. 0.0974 is above the 0.05 threshold.
  3. So you cannot reject the null of zero fixed cost.

That is not the same as proving fixed cost is zero. It means this data cannot rule zero out.

In practice it matters less here, because the firm never operates at zero volume.

Contrast the slope: t stat 7.9 and a tiny P value, so you do reject the null there. The rate is not zero.

questions.stem: Slope coefficient is $687.43 and its standard error is 87.06. What is the t stat?
questions.solution:
1. t stat = coefficient / its own standard error
  2. 687.43 / 87.06 = 7.90

A t stat is a count of standard errors away from zero. It is not a percentage.

Related: the model's F value equals the slope's t stat squared.

questions.stem: The regression has 8 observations and one independent variable. How many degrees of freedom?
questions.solution:
1. df = n − (number of parameters estimated)
  2. Simple linear regression estimates two parameters (intercept and slope), so df = n − 2
  3. 8 − 2 = 6

Multiple regression goes to n − 3, n − 4 and so on. Do not memorize "6"; memorize n minus the parameter count.

questions.stem: Slope $687.43, its standard error 87.06, df 6, t at 95% = 2.447. What is the 95% confidence interval for the variable cost rate?
questions.solution:
1. Interval = estimate ± (its own standard error × t)
  2. Half-width = 87.06 × 2.447 = 213.04
  3. Lower = 687.43 − 213.04 = $474.39
  4. Upper = 687.43 + 213.04 = $900.47

Zero is well outside this interval, which is the same conclusion the tiny P value gave.

t for 6 df: 2.447 at 95%, 1.943 at 90%. Lower confidence gives a narrower interval.

If you read the bounds straight off the ToolPak instead. Excel's Regression output prints Lower 95% and Upper 95% of 474.42 and 900.45. Those differ by about three cents from the hand calculation because Excel uses the unrounded standard error (87.0556...) while you used the printed 87.06. Either is right; the instructor builds point estimates from the printed rounded figures, so do the same and do not worry about the last few cents.

questions.stem: You need a 95% confidence interval for TOTAL COST at 400 boats. Which standard error do you use?
choices: The sum of both coefficient standard errors
questions.solution:
Use the standard error of the regression ($27,771). The professor was explicit: "I don't use either [coefficient SE]. I use the standard error for the regression as a whole."

Interval forStandard error to use
A single coefficientthat coefficient's own SE
A total-cost predictionthe regression's SE

This distinction is the most likely regression trap on the exam.

questions.stem: Total cost = $49,701.29 + $687.43 per boat. What is the point estimate of total cost at 400 boats? (Use the rounded coefficients.)
questions.solution:
1. Total cost = intercept + (slope × volume)
  2. 49,701.29 + (687.43 × 400)
  3. 49,701.29 + 274,972.00 = $324,673.29

In class the figure was $324,675.14, because Excel carries more decimals on the coefficients than the printed $687.43. The $1.85 gap is rounding, not a method error.

questions.stem: Point estimate $324,675.14 at 400 boats, regression standard error $27,771, t at 95% (6 df) = 2.447. What is the 95% interval for total cost?
questions.solution:
StepCalculationResult
Half-width2.447 × 27,771$67,955.6
Lower324,675.14 − 67,955.6$256,719
Upper324,675.14 + 67,955.6$392,631

That interval is enormous, and the professor's point is that a CEO will say so. The only two fixes: accept lower confidence, or get more data.

questions.stem: Which R measure should you report, and what is its range?
questions.solution:
Always use adjusted R squared.

MeasureRangeReads as
Multiple R (correlation)−1 to 1direction and strength
R² / adjusted R² (determination)0 to 1share of variation in Y explained by X

The professor corrected himself on this in class: correlation runs −1 to 1; R squared runs 0 to 1.

questions.stem: What is the probability that the true variable cost rate is exactly $687.43?
questions.solution:
Zero. The rate is a continuous distribution, and the probability of any single exact point under a continuous distribution is zero.

Which is the professor's larger point: every coefficient is an estimate and is "inherently and by definition wrong." That is why you work with intervals, not point estimates, and why uncertainty has to enter the decision.

questions.stem: A regression of factory cost on the number of sunspots returns a high adjusted R squared. What is the problem?
choices: Degrees of freedom are too low
Spurious correlation - the relationship makes no sense
Adjusted R squared cannot be high with one variable
questions.solution:
Spurious correlation. "Statistical tools like regression are just tools. Does it make sense?"

Regression will not tell you which costs are fixed and which are variable, and it will not tell you whether the driver is causal. That judgment is yours. Compare the session 1 lesson about a driver that is not "correlated or causally related" to the cost.

Also on the Excel mechanics: leaving the Labels box ticked when the top row is data corrupts the whole output.

questions.stem: A power bill is $1,962 at 1,300 units and $1,908 at 1,000 units. Using high-low, what is the variable rate per unit? (Enter dollars.)
questions.solution:
1. Rise = 1,962 − 1,908 = $54
  2. Run = 1,300 − 1,000 = 300 units
  3. Variable rate = 54 / 300 = $0.18 per unit

High-low fits a line through exactly two data points. A mixed cost has a fixed piece and a variable piece, and two points are enough to split it.

questions.stem: Same power bill: variable rate $0.18 per unit, total bill $1,908 at 1,000 units. What is the FIXED portion of the monthly power cost?
questions.solution:
1. Fixed = total cost at a point − (variable rate × activity at that point)
  2. 1,908 − (0.18 × 1,000)
  3. 1,908 − 180 = $1,728

"Once I have estimated M and I have a Y and an X, then I can get B."

Either data point works: 1,962 − (0.18 × 1,300) = 1,962 − 234 = $1,728.

questions.stem: Stanley's monthly fixed costs: labor $345,000/yr, fixed power $1,728/mo, occupancy $33,000/yr, administrative $600/mo, depreciation $14,355/yr. What is TOTAL monthly fixed cost?
questions.solution:

Annual amounts must be divided by 12 before they join a monthly analysis. Watch for mixed periods in the data you are given.

questions.stem: Stanley: revenue $9.00/unit, supplies $0.11/unit, variable power $0.18/unit, total monthly fixed cost $35,024.25. What is break-even in units?
questions.solution:
1. CM per unit = 9.00 − 0.11 − 0.18 = $8.71
  2. Break-even = 35,024.25 / 8.71 = 4,021.15
  3. Round up: 4,022 units

Excel showed 4,021 because it did not round. "We did 4,022 because we rounded up. Didn't matter."

Context: capacity is 4,000 units and actual demand is 1,000, so Stanley is deeply underwater.

questions.stem: Should depreciation be included in the cost analysis? The class argued about it. What was the professor's position?
choices: Exclude it - it is a non-cash accounting fiction
Include it - it is an accounting fiction that captures a real economic effect
Exclude it from break-even but include it in payback
It makes no difference either way
questions.solution:
Include it. Depreciation is "an accounting fiction" in the sense that no cash moves, but it captures something real: the asset is being used up and will need replacing.

The professor's framing: it works as a sinking fund, or a reminder to save for replacement.

In session 7 he applies this consistently: for the hammer line he prefers depreciation in, salary out. He does add it back for a cash payback calculation, because there it is the only non-cash item.

questions.stem: Giulia sells pitons at $11.00 with variable cost of $10.45 and no fixed costs, at 1,000 units/month. What is her break-even volume and monthly operating income?
questions.solution:
1. CM per unit = 11.00 − 10.45 = $0.55
  2. Break-even = FC / CM = 0 / 0.55 = 0 units
  3. Operating income = 1,000 × 0.55 = $550

Zero fixed cost means break-even is zero. Check that against intuition rather than assuming you made an error: with no fixed cost to cover, the first unit sold is profitable.

questions.stem: Scenario 3 treats labor as variable (CM $1.5725/unit, fixed $6,274.25). Scenario 4 treats the same labor as fixed (CM $8.76/unit, fixed $35,024.25; he also said $8.71 aloud, see the solution). At 4,000 units both give operating income of $15.75. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The labor treatment is irrelevant to the analysis
Profit is identical, but the risk profiles are completely different
Scenario 4 is wrong because fixed costs are too high
The scenarios must contain an arithmetic error

Profit is identical. Risk is not.

So $8.71 and 4,022 are one consistent pair, and $8.76 and $15.75 and the 22,248% change are another. Both pairs are his, from the same class. If an answer choice turns on this, look at which of the two figures the question hands you and stay inside that pair. Do not mix them.

questions.stem: Students objected to the 4,400-unit scenario. What was their objection, and was it valid?
questions.solution:
Valid objection. The scenario holds labor cost constant while raising volume 10%.

  1. The workers are already full-time at 4,000 units, which is capacity.
  2. So 4,400 units implicitly requires 10% more productivity from an unchanged labor force.
  3. If that productivity gain is not available, the $7.19 per-unit labor cost multiplies by 4,400 instead, and the economics change.

The broader lesson: cost behavior is not fate. "In some cases you can bring skills." Management choices shape whether a cost behaves as fixed or variable. Related possibility the class raised: step-fixed labor, where beyond capacity she hires temps (variable-ish) or adds salaried staff (a discrete step up in fixed cost).

Also worth naming: the case ignores financing and the forge's purchase price. The professor called that "the biggest fantasy land of all." And the contract caps her at 4,000 units plus 10%, for two years.

questions.stem: A group charged ALL 21 planes they worked on to the income statement, though only 18 were sold. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing - all production cost is expensed when incurred
The 3 unsold planes belong on the balance sheet as inventory
They should have used physical units as the denominator
They should have used a single blended rate
questions.solution:
The 3 unsold planes are capitalized cost: unexpired cost attached to units, sitting on the balance sheet as inventory (here, WIP).

TermDefinition
Costa spend
Expensean expired cost, on the income statement
Capitalizedcost attached to unexpired units; an asset

Expense only the spend attached to units sold. "Only that." Use sold, not everything that was finished.

questions.stem: Why compute three separate rates (materials, labor, overhead) rather than one blended rate per unit?
choices: Because the categories are consumed at different rates and reach different completion percentages
Because overhead must always use labor as its driver
questions.solution:
The categories "arise at different rates." In this run, materials are 100% complete on the unfinished units while labor and overhead are only 25% complete. One blended rate would misstate both the income statement and inventory.

The professor's instruction: do not "conglomerate the rates." Compute materials, labor and overhead one at a time.

Note also that the overhead driver does not have to be labor. Machine time is another option; labor is just the one used here.

questions.stem: Under absorption costing, how can a manager raise reported income without selling a single additional unit? Why does it matter?
questions.solution:
Overproduce.

  1. Absorption costing attaches labor and overhead to units.
  2. Units not sold stay in inventory on the balance sheet, carrying their share of that cost with them.
  3. So producing more than you can sell moves cost out of this period's expense and into inventory.
  4. Cost of goods sold falls, reported income rises, and nothing about the business improved.

Why it matters: current-period incentive pay layered on top of absorption costing "can cause all kinds of behaviors that ignore the downstream consequences." Two assigned papers documented it:

PaperFinding
Contemporary Accounting Research, 2011Interviews at an automaker. Managers overproduced to drive per-vehicle fixed cost down, because operating margin under absorption costing drove their performance pay. A quarter of 2004 vehicles sat over 60 days, and a $5M loss followed in 2005
Journal of Management Accounting ResearchFirms raise production relative to sales to shift fixed cost into inventory. Markets reward inventory growth, but discount the signal for repeat manipulators

State the limit: this is not a claim that absorption costing is bad. It is correct and required for external reporting. The problem is using it for a purpose it was not built for.

questions.stem: Overhead is allocated to clients on student hours. The firm drops a client, removing its revenue and its student hours. Overhead in total does not change. What happens to firm-wide profit and to the remaining clients?
choices: Profit rises; remaining clients are unaffected
Profit is unchanged; remaining clients each absorb more overhead
Profit falls by the dropped client's allocated overhead
Profit is unchanged and allocated overhead per client is unchanged
questions.solution:
Firm profit is unchanged, and the remaining clients each absorb more overhead.

  1. Allocation moves cost between cost objects. It does not change the firm's total.
  2. Total overhead stayed the same, but the denominator (total student hours) shrank, so the rate rose.
  3. Every client then looked profitable while firm profit had not moved an inch.

The professor's verdict on that rosier-looking column: "just as misleading as the other." It is "an artifact of the way that we calculated the overhead charges."

Students objected that overhead is rent and electricity, which "aren't just going to change": exactly right, and exactly the point.

questions.stem: When the professor removed a client and its student hours, total overhead went UP rather than down. What does that tell you about the driver?
choices: The allocation rate was computed incorrectly
Student hours is a poor driver - it is not correlated with or causing the cost
The cost object was defined wrongly
questions.solution:
The cost "doesn't appear to be student hours."

TermDefinition
Cost objectthe thing you are asking "what does this cost me?" about: here, a client
Driverthe activity base used to spread costs that are not directly traceable
Distortionwhat you get when the driver is not correlated with or causing the cost

A driver that fails this test produces distortion "as egregious or more" than the one you started with. Switching drivers is not automatically an improvement.

questions.stem: A colleague says the allocated-cost numbers justify holding firm on price in tomorrow's negotiation. How do you respond?
questions.solution:
Resist that call. This was the professor's most pointed warning of the semester.

  1. Allocation "just distorted the map." The allocated figure is an artifact of the driver you chose, not a fact about this client.
  2. It "might even make us behave in a negotiation in exactly the opposite way that would be the best for our business." A client that looks unprofitable under allocation may be contributing real margin.
  3. The relevant question in a negotiation is incremental: what do we gain or give up as a result of this deal? Allocated overhead does not move with the decision.

The sibling argument to resist: "we need more clients so as to spread that overhead." That is the denominator effect dressed up as strategy. Spreading a fixed amount over more units lowers cost per unit without changing any cash flow.

State the limit: "Doesn't mean we have to allocate." Full absorption is right for external GAAP reporting and for long-run pricing and product mix. It is wrong for a specific short-term decision.

questions.stem: A Reuters piece reported GM losing 'as much as $49,000' per Chevy Volt, built by spreading roughly $1.2B of development and tooling over 21,500 cars sold (about $56,000 each) and adding $20,000 to $32,000 of build cost. What is the analytical error?
choices: The development cost estimate was too high
Sunk investment and operating cost were combined in one numerator
questions.solution:
Combining sunk investment with operating cost in a single per-unit number.

  1. The $1.2B is sunk. It is "not rising and falling as I make more and fewer cars."
  2. The $20,000 to $32,000 of build cost is genuinely per-car.
  3. Dividing the first by cumulative volume and adding it to the second produces a number that describes nothing: not cash, not margin, not a decision.

Investment has its own metrics: ROI and payback. Use those for the $1.2B.

This is the denominator effect. The same fiction appears in the BYU example: cutting average credits at graduation from about 153 to 135 produces a headline saving of "over $100,000 per student" that will never show up as cash.

questions.stem: A paralegal bills $150/hour, is paid $60,000/year, and brought in almost $300,000. A partner concludes she is enormously profitable. What is missing, and what is the better question?
choices: Nothing is missing - revenue minus direct labor is the right measure
Overhead is ignored; the better question is 'if you quit, where would we be?'
Her billing rate should be allocated across clients
Her salary should be capitalized into inventory
questions.solution:
Revenue minus direct labor ignores overhead entirely. She consumes office space, support, systems and partner time.

The better question is counterfactual: "If you quit, where would we be?" That reframes it as an incremental question, which is the only form that has a decidable answer.

This is the same move as the Volt and the dropped client: ask what actually changes as a result of the decision, not what an allocation routine assigns.

questions.stem: For which purpose is full absorption costing the RIGHT approach?
choices: Deciding whether to drop a client next quarter
Setting a price in tomorrow's negotiation
External GAAP reporting and long-run pricing or product mix
Deciding whether to accept a one-off special order
questions.solution:
UseFull absorption?
External GAAP reportingYes, required
Long-run pricing and product mixYes
A specific short-term decisionNo: use incremental

Accounting software and the general ledger default to allocating everything, which answers a different question than the one you are usually asking. Do not lift a QuickBooks P&L into a decision.

The professor's recurring question: "Why do you want to know?" The right calculation depends on the answer. Management accounting is "run the business accounting, not report the business," and is not bound by GAAP, the IRS or FASB.

questions.stem: A firm pools overhead and allocates it on student hours, producing a rate of $114.02 per student hour. A client consumed 500 student hours. What overhead is allocated to that client, and what happens to firm-wide overhead?
choices: Cannot be determined without the driver total
questions.solution:
1. Allocation rate = total indirect cost pool / total driver units = $114.02 per student hour
  2. Allocated to the client = 114.02 × 500 = $57,010
  3. Firm-wide overhead: unchanged

Allocation is a distribution exercise. The pool is what it is; the rate decides who carries which slice of it. Nothing about the total moves.

questions.stem: Why does the professor leave her salary OUT of the decision analysis, and what does he say about including it?
questions.solution:
The distinguishing feature is discretion.

PointReasoning

It narrows the lensTreating the salary as the only use of the income hides the alternatives: reinvest, pay down the machine, repay debt, fund a new product

What he says about including it: it is not penalized. "You have to care about" it; he simply leaves it out of the decision analysis. Notice the asymmetry with depreciation, which he keeps in. Depreciation is not discretionary: the machine wears out whether or not she chooses to acknowledge it.

Depreciation is the only non-cash item in the analysis, so it is the only add-back. (Taxes would also matter for cash and are out of scope.)

questions.solution:

Says nothing about value after paybackIt is blind to the whole rest of the asset's life. Two projects with identical payback can differ enormously in total value

State the limit the other way too: it is still useful to her. For an owner-operator financing a machine out of a single product line's cash flow, "how many months until I have my money back" is a question she genuinely needs answered.

questions.stem: Under the allocated GAAP view, hammer gross margin is 3%. Under the incremental view it is 35%. The allocation (by productive labor time) looks arbitrary. Why does the professor say she must care about the 3% anyway?
questions.solution:
Because the two numbers answer different questions at different points in time.

ViewHammer gross marginQuestion it answers
Incremental35%Should she add hammers? (the decision point)
Allocated GAAP3%What is this business worth? (the valuation point)
  1. The decision is already made. By the time valuation matters, hammers are integrated and cannot be unwound, so the incremental question is no longer the one being asked.
  2. Capital markets run on comparability. GAAP-style allocated statements are "the currency" of that conversation.
  3. A buyer's integration differs from hers. However cleverly she reorganizes her own operation, a buyer folds the line into theirs. So what the buyer wants is comparability against the other product lines they might buy, in a "GAAP compliant, auditable way." An investor's view: it does not matter how you spread it in your operation, because I have it integrated into mine.
  4. Performance is not appearance. "I need to care about both how my firm performs, but also how it appears."

State the limits: the 3% does not mean she shouldn't add hammers. And a serious buyer will still do due diligence on contribution margin. The caution runs the other way too: "You can't anchor on this [incremental view] and say this is hammers now."

questions.stem: Pitons and hammers sell 12 to 1 by UNITS. Total revenue is $65,450, of which hammers are $21,350 (350 × $61). Break-even revenue is $54,731. What is HAMMER revenue at break-even?
questions.solution:
Split a revenue answer by the revenue mix, not the 12-to-1 unit mix.

  1. Hammer revenue share = 21,350 / 65,450 = 33% (pitons 67%)
  2. 54,731 × 33% = $18,061

The trap: the unit mix is 12 to 1, but the revenue mix is roughly 2 to 1, because a hammer sells for $61 and a piton for about $10.50. Using 1/13 of revenue for hammers would be badly wrong.

Supporting figures: his CM ratio is 82.4% (so the VC ratio is its complement, 17.6%), and break-even revenue = 45,096 / CM ratio = $54,731. Note that 45,096 / 0.824 is $54,728. His $54,731 comes from the unrounded ratio, 82.3957%. Carry the unrounded ratio and you land on his number.

Where the 33% comes from. In class he said: the unit mix was 12 to 1, but the revenue mix is 2 to 1, so he multiplied break-even revenue by 67% for pitons and 33% for hammers. $54,731 × 33% = $18,061.

The exact mix is not quite 2 : 1. Hammer revenue is $21,350 of $65,450, which is 32.62%, not 33%. Using 32.62% gives $17,853, about $208 lower. Both are defensible; his rounded 2 : 1 is the one he worked on the board. If two multiple-choice options sit about $200 apart, this is why.

questions.stem: What is 'the question' in the hammer case, and why does the professor keep returning to it?
questions.solution:
"Should she add hammers?"

He calls this the one thing to take from the course: "Remember, if you got nothing else out of the class, I hope you get this. What are we trying to answer?"

  1. It is a decision between two competing futures: add the line, or don't.
  2. A decision question makes the incremental analysis the relevant one: what is added?
  3. Every analytical choice follows from that. The salary comes out because it is discretionary. The GAAP allocation comes out because it answers a valuation question, not a decision question. Depreciation stays in because the asset really is consumed.

And the generalization, from session 1: "Why do you want to know?" The right calculation depends on the answer. Full absorption, incremental, cash: none of them is the correct view. Each is correct for a particular question.

Her final read: she should add the line. Positive incremental income, 206 units to break even against 350 expected, and a five-month payback. Family financing makes the downside less risky.

cite.quote: What is the question we're trying to answer?

questions.stem: You have just finished a multi-product CVP analysis assuming a 12-to-1 mix. What should you do next, and what should you ask about the two products?
questions.solution:
Flex the assumptions. "The minute I have this down in Excel, I know it's wrong": so the next step is sensitivity.

  1. Build cells that flex the mix: what if it is not 12 to 1?
  2. Flex the other inputs too: price, volume, salary. "You can change just about anything in there, see how it rolls through."
  3. That is what makes the decision analysis "more rich."

The question to ask about the products: are they complements or substitutes?

RelationshipImplication for the mix
ComplementsVolumes move together, up and down
SubstitutesVolumes move in opposite directions: one is sold instead of the other

That relationship governs how the mix is likely to shift, and the Goldman example shows how violently break-even responds to a mix shift: 160,000 units to 181,819 with no change in any price or cost.

(The transcript is garbled at this exact point: it reads "Complementary. Right. They're going to substitute one for the other." The distinction and its consequence are the substance; the label on this particular product pair is not recoverable from the recording.)

questions.stem: What are her short-term and long-term goals in adding the hammer line, and why does naming them matter?
questions.solution:

Why naming them matters: the goal determines which analysis is relevant.

  • "Pay off the machine" makes payback the right metric, which is why a crude, time-value-ignoring measure is defensible here.
  • "Exit, spin-off, capital markets" is what makes the allocated GAAP view matter despite looking arbitrary. A buyer needs comparability.
  • "Pay herself a salary" is precisely the item he pulls out of the decision analysis, because treating it as the only use of the income hides the alternatives.

This is the case-level version of "why do you want to know?"

questions.stem: How should you approach the short essay questions?
choices: Write everything you know about the concept so something lands

Show the full computation for each one
questions.solution:
Answer the specific question asked. The professor was explicit about both halves of this:

  2. The questions are asked specifically. "Read them carefully and make sure you're answering the right question and not just doing sort of a brain dump."

Also: the case questions are not computational and do not require recalling case details. They are about the conclusions the class reached in discussion: the "pastures we visited."
