questions.stem:
A paper airplane manufacturer reports the following for the last production period. Selling price $30 per plane. Direct material $2.50 per sheet of paper. Direct labor $16 per production period per employee (4 folders). Overhead indirect labor $16 per production period per employee (2 staffers). Overhead other $175 per production period. Airplanes started 23. Airplanes completed and sold 18. Ending work-in-process 60% complete for direct labor and overhead. No beginning inventory.

Compute operating profit for the period.
questions.solution:
Work out the units of production separately for materials and for conversion. Materials are 100% complete in work-in-process; labor and overhead are only 60% complete.

StepCalculationResult
Units of production, DM18 + 523 units
Units of production, DL and OH18 + (5 × 60%)21 units
Total DL cost$16 × 4 folders$64
Total OH cost($16 × 2 staffers) + $175$207

Now cost out only the 18 planes that were sold.

LineCalculationAmount
Revenue18 × $30$540.00
DM18 × $2.50(45.00)
DL($64 / 21) × 18(54.86)
OH($207 / 21) × 18(177.43)
Operating profit$262.72

The trap. Materials and conversion have different denominators. 23 for materials, 21 for labor and overhead. Divide everything by 23 and the profit comes out wrong.

questions.stem:
Same paper airplane period as the previous question: 23 started, 18 completed and sold, ending work-in-process 60% complete for direct labor and overhead, DM $2.50 per sheet, total DL $64, total OH $207.

Compute the value of ending inventory.
questions.solution:
Five planes are unfinished. They carry full material cost and 60% of the conversion cost.

LineCalculationAmount
DM in inventory5 × $2.50$12.50
DL in inventory($64 / 21) × (5 × 60%)9.14
OH in inventory($207 / 21) × (5 × 60%)29.57
Ending inventory balance$51.21

Check your work. What went to the income statement plus what sits in inventory must equal what was spent. 45.00 + 54.86 + 177.43 = 277.29 expensed, plus 51.21 in inventory = $328.50, which is 57.50 of materials (23 × 2.50) + 64 + 207. If those do not tie, something is wrong.

questions.stem:
Romashka, Inc. plans on introducing a new product. The marketing manager forecasts a unit selling price of $500. The variable cost per unit is estimated to be $100 per unit. In addition, there is a total of $110,000 fixed administrative support cost and $150,000 in fixed production costs associated with these units.

What quantity will the company have to sell to breakeven?
questions.solution:
Fixed costs are the two amounts together: $110,000 + $150,000 = $260,000. Both are fixed, so both belong in the same bucket.

  1. ($500 × Volume) − ($100 × Volume) − $260,000 = $0
  2. ($500 − $100) × Volume = $260,000
  3. Volume = $260,000 / $400 = 650 units

Splitting fixed cost into 'administrative' and 'production' is decoration. The home equation only cares whether a cost is fixed or variable.

questions.stem: Which of the following results in an increase in the breakeven point?
choices: Costs per unit decrease and sales price remains unchanged.
Costs per unit decrease and sales price increases.
Costs per unit remain unchanged and sales price increases.
Costs per unit increase and sales price remains unchanged.
questions.solution:
Break-even rises when contribution margin per unit falls. Only one option shrinks it.

OptionEffect on CM per unitBreak-even
Costs down, price flatupfalls
Costs down, price upupfalls
Costs flat, price upupfalls
Costs up, price flatdownrises

In the instructor's words: an increase in unit variable cost steepens the total cost line, and an increase in fixed cost shifts it up. Either one pushes break-even out.

questions.stem: Given a unit selling price of $100, fixed costs of $3,000, variable costs per unit of $75, and a total quantity of 150 units actually sold, what is the breakeven point?
questions.solution:
1. ($100 × Volume) − ($75 × Volume) − $3,000 = $0
  2. $25 × Volume = $3,000
  3. Volume = $3,000 / $25 = 120 units

The distractor. The 150 units actually sold is irrelevant to break-even. It would matter for margin of safety, not here.

questions.stem: Breakeven quantity is defined as the volume of output at which revenues are equal to:
questions.solution:
Total costs. At that volume profit is exactly zero.

Revenue − variable cost − fixed cost = 0 is the same statement as revenue = variable + fixed = total cost.

questions.stem:
Zeffer Corporation wholesales ice cream by the carton. The pro forma income statement for the current year is:

Sales $1,100,000
Cost of sales: Direct materials $100,000; Direct labor $50,000; Variable overhead $140,000; Fixed overhead $100,000 : total (390,000)
Gross profit $710,000
Selling and G&A: Variable $150,000; Fixed $150,000 : total (300,000)
Operating income $410,000

What is Zeffer's budgeted breakeven point for the upcoming year? (Round to the nearest dollar.)
questions.solution:
The income statement is laid out by cost function (cost of sales versus selling and admin). You need it by cost behavior. Re-sort every line.

BucketLinesTotal
Variable100,000 + 50,000 + 140,000 + 150,000$440,000
Fixed100,000 + 150,000$250,000
  1. Variable cost ratio = $440,000 / $1,100,000 = 0.40
  2. Revenue − 0.40(Revenue) − $250,000 = $0
  3. 0.60 × Revenue = $250,000
  4. Revenue = $250,000 / 0.60 = $416,666.67, which rounds to $416,667

The trap. Fixed overhead sits inside cost of sales and variable selling sits below gross profit. Anyone who treats 'cost of sales' as variable and 'selling and G&A' as fixed gets a wrong answer. Sort by behavior, never by where the line sits.

questions.stem:
Western Wear Co. is launching a new line of shirts. Unit costs: Direct Materials $9.25, Direct Labor $4.00, Distribution $1.75, all variable. The company will incur $180,000 of additional fixed costs associated with this new product. A corporate fixed charge of $30,000 currently absorbed by other products will be allocated to this new product (on top of the $180,000).

If the selling price is $24 per unit, the breakeven point in units (rounded to the nearest hundred) for shirts is:
questions.solution:
The $30,000 corporate charge is allocated, not avoidable. It is already being paid by other products and does not change because this line exists. Leave it out.

  1. Variable cost per unit = $9.25 + $4.00 + $1.75 = $15
  2. Avoidable fixed cost = $180,000
  3. ($24 × Volume) − ($15 × Volume) − $180,000 = $0
  4. $9 × Volume = $180,000, so Volume = 20,000 units

Including the $30,000 gives $210,000 / $9 = 23,333 units, which is the planted wrong answer.

questions.stem: What aspect of C-V-P analysis is represented by the number of units produced or the number of units sold?
choices: The activity level in the business process
The behavior of costs (fixed versus variable)
The contribution margin that covers fixed costs
The target profit for the organization
questions.solution: The activity level. In the instructor's own statement of the formula: Sales Price × Activity − VC Rate × Activity − Total Fixed Cost = Profit: the term that units fill is 'Activity'.

questions.stem: Breeze Company has a contribution margin of $4,000 and fixed costs of $1,000. If the total contribution margin increases by $1,000, operating profit would:
questions.solution:
Increase by $1,000. Fixed costs do not move, so every extra dollar of contribution margin falls straight to operating profit, one for one.

The $4,000 and $1,000 starting figures are not needed. This is the whole point of the contribution margin format: it isolates the dollars that are free to cover fixed cost and then become profit.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements accurately describes the cost behavior of fixed costs in response to changes in business volume levels that take place within the relevant range of activity?
choices: Total fixed costs change with increases or decreases in volume.
Total fixed costs remain constant within the relevant range of activity.
Fixed costs on a total and per unit basis both remain constant within the relevant range of activity.
Fixed costs on a total and per-unit basis both change with increases or decreases in volume.
questions.solution:
Total fixed cost holds still; fixed cost per unit does not.

In totalPer unit
Fixed costconstantchanges (falls as volume rises)
Variable costchangesconstant

This is exactly why the instructor puts a red 'no' symbol on the fixed-cost-per-unit cell of his income statement. A fixed cost per unit is only true at one volume.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements accurately describes the cost behavior of variable costs in response to changes in business volume levels that take place within the relevant range of activity?
choices: Variable costs per unit change with increases or decreases in volume.
Variable costs on a total and per-unit basis both remain constant within the relevant range of activity.
Variable costs on a total and per-unit basis both change with increases or decreases in volume.
Variable costs on a per-unit basis remain constant.
questions.solution:
Variable cost per unit is constant; total variable cost moves with volume.

Same table as the fixed-cost question, read along the other row. The two behave in mirror image, and almost every cost-behavior question on this exam is testing whether you can keep the mirror straight.

questions.stem:
Pet Friends Products has a new electronic dog collar. Variable manufacturing costs are $30 per unit with monthly fixed costs of $50,000. Three marketing plans:

Plan A: sell online at $50 per unit, no additional selling costs, customer pays shipping. Estimated monthly sales 4,200 units.
Plan B: sell through company retail stores in special packaging costing $5 per unit, plus $10,000 additional fixed monthly costs. Sales price $55. Estimated monthly sales 5,500 units.
Plan C: sell using commissioned sales reps. Special packaging $5 per unit, no additional fixed costs, sales commission 15% on the sales price of $60. Estimated monthly sales 6,000 units.

Rank the three plans in order of operating income from lowest to highest.
choices: Plan A, Plan B, Plan C
Plan C, Plan B, Plan A
Plan B, Plan A, Plan C
Plan A, Plan C, Plan B
questions.solution:
Get contribution margin per unit first, then subtract each plan's own fixed costs.

PlanCM per unitOperating income
A$50 − $30 = $20($20 × 4,200) − $50,000 = $34,000
B$55 − $30 − $5 = $20($20 × 5,500) − $50,000 − $10,000 = $50,000
C$60 − $30 − $5 − ($60 × 15%) = $16($16 × 6,000) − $50,000 = $46,000

Lowest to highest is A, C, B.

The trap. A commission quoted as a percentage of price is a variable cost. $60 × 15% = $9 per unit. Plan C has the highest price and the highest volume and still loses to B.

questions.stem:
Swimtech produces racing swim goggles. Cost structure shifts across relevant ranges:

Units produced/sold1,000-5,9996,000-10,99911,000-15,99916,000-20,000
Total fixed costs$200,000$400,000$600,000$800,000
Unit variable cost$50$50$45$45
Unit sales price$100$100$100$100

Which production and sales level produces the highest operating income?
questions.solution:
Each volume sits in a different relevant range, so look up that range's own fixed cost and variable rate.

VolumeCM per unitFixedOperating income
8,000$50$400,000$0
11,000$55$600,000$5,000
14,000$55$600,000$170,000
17,000$55$800,000$135,000

14,000 wins: ($100 − $45) × 14,000 − $600,000 = $170,000.

The lesson. More volume is not always more profit. Crossing into the next range adds $200,000 of fixed cost, and 17,000 units does not generate enough extra contribution to cover it.

questions.stem:
Alton Industries is considering a new product requiring a $500,000 investment of capital, funded by a bank loan at 10%. Fixed operating costs would be $200,000 and the contribution margin percentage would be 35%. Selling price is $30 per unit.

Determine the number of units Alton would have to sell to generate earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) of 25% of the capital invested. (Round to the nearest unit.)
questions.solution:
1. Required EBIT = 25% × $500,000 = $125,000
  2. CM per unit = $30 × 35% = $10.50
  3. $10.50 × Units − $200,000 = $125,000
  4. Units = $325,000 / $10.50 = 30,952.38, so 30,952 units

Why the 10% interest is a decoy. The target is stated on EBIT, earnings before interest. Interest sits below that line, so it never enters the computation. The instructor's own note says the interest charge is not a cost factor in this solution.

questions.stem:
Kipper Company has set the price for its single product at $50 per unit. The contribution margin ratio is 30%, and fixed costs are $10,000. Sales were 3,000 units in June and 4,000 units in July.

How much greater is the July operating income than the June operating income?
questions.solution:
1. Extra revenue = 1,000 extra units × $50 = $50,000
  2. Change in operating income = $50,000 × 0.30 = $15,000

Why fixed cost is ignored. The $10,000 is the same in both months, so it cancels in the difference. When a question asks for a change in profit, you only need contribution margin.

questions.stem:
Pratt & Sons produces fly fishing equipment. Last year the company produced and sold 15,000 standard fishing reels at $185 per unit. Variable costs were $65 per unit, and fixed costs were $75 per unit. Marketing estimates 18,000 units for the upcoming year, within the relevant range.

What is the breakeven point in units and the expected operating profit for the upcoming year?
choices: 11,250 units to breakeven and $810,000 in operating profit
17,308 units to breakeven and $45,000 in operating profit
8,599 units to breakeven and $1,230,000 in operating profit
9,375 units to breakeven and $1,035,000 in operating profit
questions.solution:
The $75 is fixed cost per unit at last year's volume. Convert it to a total before using it.

  1. Total fixed cost = $75 × 15,000 = $1,125,000
  2. CM per unit = $185 − $65 = $120
  3. Break-even = $1,125,000 / $120 = 9,375 units
  4. Operating income at 18,000 = ($120 × 18,000) − $1,125,000 = $1,035,000

The trap, and it is the single most common one. If you treat $75 as a per-unit cost at the new volume you get CM of $45 and break-even of 17,308 : which is sitting right there as a wrong answer. Fixed cost per unit is only valid at the volume where it was computed.

questions.stem:
The financial analyst calculates that the breakeven point in revenue for a product is $250,000. The product sells for $25 per unit. Fixed costs are $100,000.

What is the contribution margin per unit?
questions.solution:
Work backwards from break-even, where profit is zero and revenue equals total cost.

  1. $250,000 − Variable costs − $100,000 = $0, so variable costs = $150,000
  2. Units = $250,000 / $25 = 10,000 units
  3. Variable cost per unit = $150,000 / 10,000 = $15.00
  4. CM per unit = $25.00 − $15.00 = $10.00

Shortcut worth knowing: CM per unit = fixed cost / break-even units = $100,000 / 10,000 = $10.00.

questions.stem:
Arvin Tax Preparation Services has annual budgeted revenues of $618,000, based on an average price of $206 per tax return. Fixed costs are $326,600 and variable costs average $64 per tax return.

Calculate Arvin's break-even point and margin of safety in units.
choices: Break-even point is 2,300 tax returns; margin of safety is 3,000 tax returns
Break-even point is 2,300 tax returns; margin of safety is 700 tax returns
Break-even point is 1,586 tax returns; margin of safety is 1,414 tax returns
Break-even point is 1,586 tax returns; margin of safety is 3,000 tax returns
questions.solution:
1. $206(Volume) − $64(Volume) − $326,600 = $0
  2. $142(Volume) = $326,600, so break-even = 2,300 returns
  3. Current volume = $618,000 / $206 = 3,000 returns
  4. Margin of safety = 3,000 − 2,300 = 700 returns

Two steps people skip. The question gives revenue, not volume, so you have to divide to get the 3,000. And margin of safety is a difference, not the break-even itself. Option A hands you the current volume as if it were the margin of safety.

questions.stem:
Rhetorix, Inc. produces stereo speakers. The selling price per pair is $1,000. Variable cost of production is $300 and fixed cost per month is $49,000. For November the company expects to sell 125 pairs.

Calculate the margin of safety in dollars.
questions.solution:
1. Variable cost ratio = $300 / $1,000 = 30%
  2. Revenue − 0.30(Revenue) − $49,000 = $0
  3. 0.70(Revenue) = $49,000, so break-even revenue = $70,000
  4. Current revenue = $1,000 × 125 = $125,000
  5. Margin of safety = $125,000 − $70,000 = $55,000

Both wrong answers are real numbers from the problem: $70,000 is the break-even and $125,000 is current sales. The margin of safety is the gap between them.

questions.stem:
Edison Entrepreneur Services charges $1,200 per incorporation application and plans to file 1,600 applications next year.

Sales $1,920,000
less Variable expenses (1,152,000)
Contribution margin 768,000
less Fixed expenses (300,000)
Operating income $468,000

What is the margin of safety in units and in sales dollars?
choices: Margin of safety in units is 1,350 applications; in sales dollars is $1,620,000
Margin of safety in units is 625 applications; in sales dollars is $750,000
Margin of safety in units is 1,600 applications; in sales dollars is $1,920,000
Margin of safety in units is 975 applications; in sales dollars is $1,170,000
questions.solution:
1. Variable cost per application = $1,152,000 / 1,600 = $720
  2. $1,200(Volume) − $720(Volume) − $300,000 = $0
  3. $480(Volume) = $300,000, so break-even = 625 applications, or 625 × $1,200 = $750,000
  4. Margin of safety = 1,600 − 625 = 975 applications
  5. In dollars = 975 × $1,200 = $1,170,000

Option B is the break-even itself, which is the most common miss on this question.

questions.stem:
MathTot sells a learning system. Based on sales of 12,000 lessons, last month's income statement was:

Sales $600,000
less Variable expenses 210,000
Contribution margin $390,000
less Fixed expenses 292,500
Operating income $97,500

What is MathTot's margin of safety in sales revenue?
questions.solution:
1. Price = $600,000 / 12,000 = $50.00 per lesson
  2. Variable cost = $210,000 / 12,000 = $17.50 per lesson
  3. $50.00(Volume) − $17.50(Volume) − $292,500 = $0
  4. $32.50(Volume) = $292,500, so break-even = 9,000 lessons, or $450,000 of revenue
  5. Margin of safety = $600,000 − $450,000 = $150,000

questions.stem:
MathTot again: 12,000 lessons, sales $600,000, variable expenses $210,000, fixed expenses $292,500. Managers have determined that variable costs per unit will increase by 16% next month. To offset this they are considering a 10% increase in the sales price. Market research indicates the price increase will cause a 2% decrease in the number of systems sold.

What is the effect on the margin of safety, measured in lessons?
choices: The margin of safety will decrease by 849 lessons.
The margin of safety will increase by 960 lessons.
The margin of safety will increase by 330 lessons.
The margin of safety will increase by 570 lessons.
questions.solution:
Three things move at once. Recompute the whole margin of safety, do not try to adjust the old one.

NowNext month
Price$50.00$50.00 × 1.10 = $55.00
Variable cost$17.50$17.50 × 1.16 = $20.30
CM per unit$32.50$34.70
Volume12,00012,000 × 0.98 = 11,760
Break-even9,000292,500 / 34.70 = 8,429.4 → 8,430
Margin of safety3,0003,330

Increase = 3,330 − 3,000 = 330 lessons.

Rounding matters here. He rounds break-even up: 8,429.4 becomes 8,430. Rounding down would give 3,331 and a 331 increase, which is not an option.

questions.stem:
TRC Company sells personalized water bottles for $50 each. TRC buys the bottles for $16, the logo decals for $13, and spends $4 in variable selling and administrative costs per bottle. All other costs are fixed. The GAAP results of last month:

Sales Revenue $750,000
Cost of Goods Sold (570,000)
Gross Margin 180,000
Selling & Admin Expenses (112,500)
Operating Income $67,500

What are monthly total fixed costs?
questions.solution:
Total cost splits into variable and fixed. Find total cost, find variable, subtract.

  1. Units = $750,000 / $50 = 15,000
  2. Variable cost per unit = $16 + $13 + $4 = $33
  3. Total variable cost = $33 × 15,000 = $495,000
  4. Total cost = $570,000 + $112,500 = $682,500
  5. Total fixed cost = $682,500 − $495,000 = $187,500

The trap. Cost of goods sold is not the variable cost and selling and admin is not the fixed cost. Both lines are mixtures. You must rebuild the split from the per-unit data given.

questions.stem:
Robinson Company sells personalized sports decals for $5 each. Robinson buys the decals for $1.50 and spends $0.30 in variable operating costs per decal. All other costs are fixed. Last month:

Sales Revenue $20,000
Less Cost of Goods Sold (8,000)
Gross Profit $12,000
Less Operating Expenses (7,400)
Operating Income $4,600

Robinson wants to know how far above the breakeven point current sales are. What is the margin of safety percentage?
questions.solution:
1. Units = $20,000 / $5.00 = 4,000
  2. Variable cost per unit = $1.50 + $0.30 = $1.80
  3. Total fixed = $8,000 + $7,400 − (4,000 × $1.80) = $8,200
  4. $5.00(Volume) − $1.80(Volume) − $8,200 = $0
  5. $3.20(Volume) = $8,200, so break-even = 2,562.5 → 2,563 units (round up)
  6. Margin of safety = 4,000 − 2,563 = 1,437 units
  7. Margin of safety % = 1,437 / 2,563 = 56.07%

This question settles which denominator to use. The words 'how far above the breakeven point' mean you divide by break-even, not by current sales. Dividing by current sales gives 1,437 / 4,000 = 36%, which is sitting there as option C. The other phrasing, 'how far can sales fall', is the one that divides by current sales.

questions.stem:
Justin Lake sells one style of baseball hat, buying at $13 and selling at $18. His current breakeven point is 15,000 hats per year. Based on a 30% income tax rate, he projects an after-tax profit of $14,000.

What is Justin's current margin of safety in sales revenue?
questions.solution:
Back out fixed cost from the break-even, gross up the after-tax target, then solve for volume.

  1. $18(15,000) − $13(15,000) − Fixed = $0, so fixed = $270,000 − $195,000 = $75,000
  2. Pretax profit = $14,000 / (1 − 0.30) = $20,000
  3. $18(Volume) − $13(Volume) − $75,000 = $20,000
  4. $5(Volume) = $95,000, so volume = 19,000 hats
  5. Margin of safety = 19,000 − 15,000 = 4,000 hats, or 4,000 × $18 = $72,000

Note that $75,000 (the fixed cost) and $20,000 (the pretax profit) are both planted as wrong answers. They are real intermediate numbers, which is what makes them tempting.

questions.stem:
DMT, Inc. manufactures gas tanks. Sales price per unit is $430 and variable costs per unit are $180. Total fixed costs are $1,400,000. The controller performed a sensitivity analysis on a $30 per unit direct labor decrease and a $250,000 increase in fixed costs.

How will the breakeven point be affected? (Round to the nearest unit.)
questions.solution:
OriginalNew
CM per unit$430 − $180 = $250$430 − $150 = $280
Fixed cost$1,400,000$1,650,000
Break-even5,600 units5,892.86 → 5,893 units

Change = 5,893 − 5,600 = increase of 293 units.

Why it goes up even though unit cost fell. Trading variable cost for fixed cost is the classic operating-leverage move. It raises contribution margin per unit, but the larger fixed base has to be covered first, so break-even moves out. Profit above break-even now grows faster, and losses below it grow faster too.

questions.stem:
MultiFrame Company sells two products.

Plastic FramesGlass Frames
Sales price$10.00$15.00
Direct materials2.003.00
Direct labor3.005.00
Fixed overhead3.004.00
Net income per unit$2.00$3.00
Budgeted unit sales100,000300,000

Total fixed overhead is budgeted at $975,000 and the mix stays proportional.

The total number of frames needed to break even is:
questions.solution:
The fixed overhead per unit ($3 and $4) is not a variable cost. Strip it out. Variable cost is materials plus labor only: $5 and $8.

  1. Unit mix = 100,000 : 300,000 = 1 : 3
  2. Basket price = 1 × $10 + 3 × $15 = $55
  3. Basket variable cost = 1 × $5 + 3 × $8 = $29
  4. $55(Baskets) − $29(Baskets) − $975,000 = $0
  5. $26(Baskets) = $975,000, so 37,500 baskets
  6. Unpack: 37,500 plastic + 112,500 glass = 150,000 total frames

Read the question. It asks for the total. 37,500 is the basket count and also the plastic count; 112,500 is the glass count. All three are offered as answers.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements does not describe the analysis of multiple products?
choices: In a business condition with multiple products, there is one unique combination of units for a breakeven point.
The number of units for a breakeven point depends on the fixed and variable costs and total sales.
A shift from low-margin items to high-margin items can cause operating income to rise even though total sales may decrease.
A shift from high-margin items to low-margin items can cause operating income to fall even though total sales may increase.
questions.solution:
The false statement is the first one. There is no unique multi-product break-even.

Every multi-product break-even is conditional on an assumed sales mix. Change the mix and you get a different answer, as the Goldman problem shows: the same 200,000 units break even at 160,000 under one mix and 181,819 under another. The instructor's phrasing is that the sales mix assumption is huge.

A mathematical solution does produce one specific combination for a given mix, but management can reach break-even through many different mixes.

questions.stem:
Simon's Wholesale Flowers sells simple and upgraded bouquets. Total fixed costs are $184,000.

SimpleUpgraded
Selling price per unit$24.00$40.00
Variable cost per unit$20.00$32.00
Budgeted sales (units)20,00030,000

How many bouquets are required to reach the breakeven point?
questions.solution:
1. Unit mix = 20,000 : 30,000 = 2 : 3
  2. Basket price = 2 × $24 + 3 × $40 = $168
  3. Basket variable cost = 2 × $20 + 3 × $32 = $136
  4. $32(Baskets) = $184,000, so 5,750 baskets
  5. Unpack: 5,750 × 2 = 11,500 simple; 5,750 × 3 = 17,250 upgraded

Option B splits the total evenly between the two products, which ignores the mix entirely. That is the error the basket method exists to prevent.

questions.stem:
Simon's Wholesale Flowers, same data: simple $24 price and $20 variable cost, upgraded $40 price and $32 variable cost, total fixed costs $184,000.

If the mix changes to three upgraded for each simple, the breakeven volume for each product would be:
questions.solution:
1. New unit mix = 1 : 3
  2. Basket price = 1 × $24 + 3 × $40 = $144
  3. Basket variable cost = 1 × $20 + 3 × $32 = $116
  4. $28(Baskets) = $184,000, so 6,571.4 baskets
  5. Unpack: 6,571.4 × 1 = 6,571.4 → 6,572 simple; 6,571.4 × 3 = 19,714.3 → 19,715 upgraded

Rounding, exactly as he does it. The basket count is left unrounded at 6,571.4. You unpack first, then round each product up. Rounding the baskets to 6,572 before unpacking gives 19,716 upgraded, which is wrong.

Compare with the previous question. Total bouquets at break even fell from 28,750 to 26,287, because the mix moved toward the upgraded bouquet, which carries the fatter margin on both measures: $8 per unit against $4, and 20.0% against 16.7%.

The basket count still rose, 5,750 to 6,571.4, and that is the part worth holding. The basket itself shrank from 5 bouquets to 4, so it takes more baskets to cover the same fixed cost even though each bouquet now contributes more. Baskets are a counting device, not a quantity. Never read a trend off the basket count. Unpack to units first.

questions.stem:
Magan Company carries three household cleaning products: Waxen, Buffo and Bright. Waxen has the highest contribution margin and Bright the lowest.

Which event will definitely increase the firm's overall breakeven point?
choices: An increase in Bright's selling price
A decrease in anticipated sales of Waxen relative to sales of Buffo and Bright
A decrease in Waxen's raw material cost
The installation of new computer-controlled machinery and subsequent layoff of assembly-line workers
questions.solution:
A shift in mix away from the highest-margin product lowers the overall contribution margin, which raises break-even. That is the only option guaranteed to push it up.

OptionEffect
Bright's price upCM up, break-even falls
Mix away from Waxenoverall CM down, break-even rises
Waxen's material cost downCM up, break-even falls
Machinery replaces laborfixed up, variable down: direction is ambiguous

The last option is the tempting one. Swapping labor for machinery raises fixed cost but also raises contribution margin per unit, so break-even can move either way. 'Definitely' rules it out.

questions.stem:
Noosh Enterprises has prepared this budget for July. Total fixed costs will be $150,000 and the sales mix remains constant.

Selling PriceVariable CostUnit Sales
Product A$10.00$4.0014,000
Product B16.008.0020,000
Product C18.009.0010,000

What is the breakeven point in total sales dollars (rounded to the next penny)?
questions.solution:
Asked for dollars, so use the revenue approach: build the overall variable cost ratio.

ProductRevenueVariable cost
A$10 × 14,000 = $140,000$4 × 14,000 = $56,000
B$16 × 20,000 = $320,000$8 × 20,000 = $160,000
C$18 × 10,000 = $180,000$9 × 10,000 = $90,000
Total$640,000$306,000
  1. Variable cost ratio = $306,000 / $640,000 = 0.478125
  2. Revenue − 0.478125(Revenue) − $150,000 = $0
  3. Revenue = $150,000 / (1 − 0.478125) = $287,425.15

To split it by product, use the revenue mix: A 21.875%, B 50.000%, C 28.125%. Do not use the unit mix for a dollar answer.

questions.stem:
Animal Life Theater is planning its summer season.

ProductionVC/ticketFixed costsPerformancesAvg attendanceTicket price
The Beautiful Beast$4.00$80,000101,200$16.00
Looking for Charlotte$3.00$120,000121,500$15.00
The Seal Prince$4.00$180,00082,000$22.00

The theater also incurs $120,000 of fixed costs for administrative overhead and facilities. How many total tickets must it sell to earn $100,000 before tax? (Round up to the nearest ticket.)
questions.solution:
Build the mix from performances × attendance, and pool every fixed cost including the production-specific ones.

  1. Tickets: Beast 10 × 1,200 = 12,000; Charlotte 12 × 1,500 = 18,000; Seal 8 × 2,000 = 16,000. Mix is 12 : 18 : 16
  2. Basket price = 12($16) + 18($15) + 16($22) = $814
  3. Basket variable cost = 12($4) + 18($3) + 16($4) = $166
  4. Total fixed = $80,000 + $120,000 + $180,000 + $120,000 = $500,000
  5. $648(Baskets) = $500,000 + $100,000, so 925.926 baskets
  6. Unpack: 11,111.2 + 16,666.7 + 14,814.9 = 42,592.8 → 42,593 tickets

Two traps. The three production fixed costs are easy to miss because they sit in the product table rather than below it. And the target profit goes in the numerator alongside fixed cost, not anywhere else.

questions.stem: National Consulting has two teams. Contribution margin per consulting hour is $80 for the A Team and $100 for the B Team. If the sales mix shifts towards Team B, which statement is correct?
choices: The contribution margin ratio for Team B will increase.
The overall contribution margin ratio for National Consulting will decrease.
If the total number of consulting hours sold remains the same, the operating income will increase.
The total number of consulting hours to break even will increase.
questions.solution:
Shifting hours from the $80 team to the $100 team raises the average contribution margin per hour. At the same total hours, operating income rises.

OptionWhy it fails
Team B's CM ratio risesTeam B's own ratio is a property of Team B. A mix shift does not change it.
Overall CM ratio fallsBackwards. It rises.
Hours to break even riseBackwards. A higher average CM means fewer hours needed.

The distinction worth holding: a mix shift changes the blended figures, never the individual product's own margin.

questions.stem:
Finn Products wants cost-based pricing for its only product. Finn expects to sell 10,000 units next year. Variable costs are $65 per unit and annual fixed operating costs (including depreciation) are $80,000. The balance sheet shows current assets $100,000, plant and equipment $425,000, accounts payable $25,000, debt $200,000 and equity $300,000.

What price is needed if Finn wants a 20% return on equity (ROE) and the tax rate is 25%?
questions.solution:
Three moves: turn the return target into after-tax dollars, gross it up to pretax, then solve the home equation for price.

  1. After-tax income = Equity × ROE = $300,000 × 20% = $60,000
  2. Before-tax income = $60,000 / (1 − 0.25) = $80,000
  3. Price(10,000) − $65(10,000) − $80,000 = $80,000
  4. Price(10,000) = $650,000 + $80,000 + $80,000 = $810,000
  5. Price = $810,000 / 10,000 = $81.00 per unit

Almost everything on that balance sheet is a decoy. ROE uses equity, so only the $300,000 matters. Total assets, debt and payables are there to see whether you know which denominator the ratio uses. If the target had been ROA you would use $525,000 instead.

questions.stem:
Carson Inc. manufactures one product. Selling price $100 per unit, variable costs $75 per unit, fixed costs $250,000, effective tax rate 35%.

If Carson wants a net after-tax income of $1.3 million next year, its sales must be:
questions.solution:
1. Pretax profit = $1,300,000 / (1 − 0.35) = $2,000,000
  2. $100(Units) − $75(Units) − $250,000 = $2,000,000
  3. $25(Units) = $2,250,000
  4. Units = 90,000

Gross up, never gross down. Dividing by (1 − t) makes the target bigger, because you must earn more than $1.3 million pretax to keep $1.3 million after tax. Multiplying by (1 − 0.35) instead gives $845,000 pretax and 43,800 units, which is not even offered.

questions.stem:
Delphi Company's new product can be sold at up to 35,000 units at $36, but capacity is capped at 25,000 units annually. Fixed costs are budgeted at $450,000 including $60,000 of depreciation. Variable costs per unit: direct material $7.00, direct labor $3.50, manufacturing overhead $4.00 (total variable manufacturing $14.50), selling expenses $1.50, total variable $16.00. Tax rate 40%.

Management will not continue the product unless after-tax profit is at least $75,000 in the first year. The unit selling price to achieve this must be at least:
questions.solution:
1. Pretax profit = $75,000 / (1 − 0.40) = $125,000
  2. Volume is the capacity of 25,000, not the 35,000 the market would absorb
  3. Price(25,000) − $16(25,000) − $450,000 = $125,000
  4. Price(25,000) = $400,000 + $450,000 + $125,000 = $975,000
  5. Price = $975,000 / 25,000 = $39.00

Two traps. Use 25,000 units, since you cannot sell what you cannot make. And use the full $16.00 variable cost, not the $14.50 manufacturing subtotal: selling expenses are variable too. The $60,000 of depreciation is already inside the $450,000 and is not deducted again.

questions.stem:
Carl's Corp faces competition driving price from $60 to $50 per unit. If it matches the new price, sales rise from 700,000 to 800,000 units. Current variable cost per unit is $45 and total fixed costs are $500,000.

To maintain a 25% target contribution margin on sales revenue, the company must lower its variable production costs by how much?
questions.solution:
1. New revenue = $50 × 800,000 = $40,000,000
  2. Target contribution margin = 25% × $40,000,000 = $10,000,000
  3. $40,000,000 − (Variable cost × 800,000) = $10,000,000
  4. Variable cost × 800,000 = $30,000,000, so variable cost = $37.50 per unit
  5. Reduction = $45.00 − $37.50 = $7.50 per unit

The $500,000 of fixed cost never enters. A contribution margin target stops above the fixed-cost line. Notice also that a 25% CM ratio on a $50 price simply means CM of $12.50 per unit, so variable cost must be $37.50. Both routes give the same answer.

questions.stem:
Allied Games expects to sell a new game at $4.50 per download. Estimated costs at a production of 300,000 copies: code programming $68,000; testing $55,000; depreciation on technical equipment $11,000; administrative $13,000; marketing $50,000; sales team commissions (3% of selling price) $40,500; distribution commissions (25% of selling price) $337,500; game designer royalties (12% of selling price) $162,000.

The only variable costs are the commissions and royalties. How many downloads must Allied sell to generate operating earnings of 25% of sales revenue? (Round up.)
questions.solution:
1. Variable cost per download = ($40,500 + $337,500 + $162,000) / 300,000 = $1.80
  2. Total fixed = $68,000 + $55,000 + $11,000 + $13,000 + $50,000 = $197,000
  3. Profit target = 25% × ($4.50 × Downloads) = $1.125 × Downloads
  4. ($4.50 − $1.80) × Downloads − $197,000 = $1.125 × Downloads
  5. $2.70D − $1.125D = $197,000, so $1.575D = $197,000
  6. D = 125,079.37 → 125,080 downloads

The move that makes this question. When the target is a percentage of revenue, it carries the unknown in it. Put it on the right-hand side and collect the Downloads terms on the left. You cannot just add it to fixed cost the way you would a dollar target.

The commissions are given as totals at 300,000 copies, so divide to get the per-unit rate. Alternatively 3% + 25% + 12% = 40% of $4.50 = $1.80, which is the same thing.

questions.stem:
Baird Soccer Balls has invested $300,000 in new technology. Variable costs will be 20% of the selling price, annual fixed costs $400,000, effective income tax rate 40%.

What sales revenue is required to earn a 10% after-tax annual return on its investment?
questions.solution:
1. After-tax income target = $300,000 × 10% = $30,000
  2. Pretax income target = $30,000 / (1 − 0.40) = $50,000
  3. Revenue − 20%(Revenue) − $400,000 = $50,000
  4. 80%(Revenue) = $450,000
  5. Revenue = $450,000 / 0.80 = $562,500

Because variable cost is given as a percentage of price, use the revenue form of the home equation. There is no unit price here and none is needed.

questions.stem: All of the following are common management uses for C-V-P analysis except:
choices: Determining whether to invest in technology to replace manual labor
questions.solution:
Quality control specifications. That work is about acceptable error rates in a process, which is production design and statistics, not cost-volume-profit.

The other three are all CVP questions in disguise. Technology for labor is a fixed-for-variable swap. Pricing sets the contribution margin. Outsourcing converts fixed cost to a per-unit cost, which is precisely the TenAlpina Case 1 question.

questions.stem:
Two production processes are being analyzed for a product selling at $120 per unit, with 10,000 units projected annually.

Process A: $55 per unit variable cost, annual fixed costs $200,000.
Process B: $50 per unit variable cost, annual fixed costs $325,000.

Target income is $400,000. What should the team recommend?
choices: Reject both production processes. Neither process will achieve the target income.
Accept either process. Both processes will achieve the target income.
Accept Process A and reject Process B. Only Process A will achieve the target income.
Accept Process B and reject Process A. Only Process B will achieve the target income.
questions.solution:
ProcessCM per unitOperating income at 10,000Meets $400,000?
A$120 − $55 = $65($65 × 10,000) − $200,000 = $450,000yes
B$120 − $50 = $70($70 × 10,000) − $325,000 = $375,000no

Accept A. B has the better contribution margin per unit and still loses, because the extra $125,000 of fixed cost outweighs the extra $5 per unit at this volume. $5 × 10,000 = $50,000 of extra contribution against $125,000 of extra fixed cost.

B would win at higher volume. The indifference point is where $5 × Volume = $125,000, i.e. 25,000 units. Below that, A; above that, B.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the high-low method and regression analysis?
choices: When using the high-low method, only two data points are used, which is a strength. When using regression analysis, all data points are used, which is a weakness.
When using the high-low method, only two data points are used, which is a weakness. When using regression analysis, all data points are used, which is a strength.
When using the high-low method, all data points are used, which is a weakness. When using regression analysis, only two data points are used, which is a strength.
When using the high-low method, all data points are used, which is a strength. When using regression analysis, only two data points are used, which is a weakness.
questions.solution:
High-low uses two points, and that is its limitation. Regression uses all points, and that is its strength.

The instructor's framing: high-low 'focuses strictly on using just two data points and essentially ignores the rest of the data'. Regression 'plots a line of best fit between all data points', where the slope is the variable cost and the y-intercept is the total fixed cost.

High-low's compensating virtue is that you can do it on paper in thirty seconds, which is why it is still on the exam.

questions.stem:
Dana's real estate agency wants to split advertising cost into variable and fixed components.

MonthListingsAdvertising Cost
March35$23,145
April23$15,025
May22$15,280
June42$27,205
July48$30,565
August51$32,485
September50$31,835
October56$36,020
November54$36,920

Using the high-low method, what is Dana's fixed cost for advertising?
questions.solution:
Pick the high and low by the activity driver, which is listings, not by cost. Highest listings is October at 56. Lowest is May at 22.

  1. Variable cost = ($36,020 − $15,280) / (56 − 22) = $20,740 / 34 = $610 per listing
  2. Fixed cost = $36,020 − (56 × $610) = $36,020 − $34,160 = $1,860
  3. Check with the low point: $15,280 − (22 × $610) = $15,280 − $13,420 = $1,860 ✓

The trap is deliberate. November has the highest cost ($36,920) but only 54 listings, and April has a lower cost than May despite more listings. Choosing by cost gives ($36,920 − $15,025) / (54 − 23) = $706.29 and a different fixed cost. Always sort on the driver.

One wrinkle in the instructor's own solution file: it writes 'Using May's data' and then substitutes October's 56 listings and $36,020. The arithmetic and the answer are right; only the month label is a slip.

questions.stem:
Children's World sold 4,000 Donny the Dragon stuffed toys in April and 6,000 in May. Shipping costs for the two months were $12,000 and $16,800.

Using the high-low method on these two months, the fixed cost is estimated as:
questions.solution:
1. Variable cost = ($16,800 − $12,000) / (6,000 − 4,000) = $4,800 / 2,000 = $2.40 per toy
  2. Fixed cost = $12,000 − (4,000 × $2.40) = $12,000 − $9,600 = $2,400
  3. Check: $16,800 − (6,000 × $2.40) = $16,800 − $14,400 = $2,400 ✓

Option B, $4,800, is the change in cost. Option A is the variable cost times 1,000. Always finish by checking the intercept at both points; if they disagree you made an arithmetic error.

questions.stem:
Ramirez Company makes leather jackets selling for $175 each. The total cost in May of manufacturing 1,000 jackets is $114,860. The variable cost for each jacket is $57.

What are Ramirez's fixed costs for the month?
questions.solution:
1. Total variable cost = 1,000 × $57 = $57,000
  2. Fixed cost = $114,860 − $57,000 = $57,860

The $175 price is not needed. This is the total cost equation read backwards: Total cost = variable rate × volume + total fixed, so fixed = total − variable.

questions.stem:
A product sells for $50 per unit, with variable manufacturing costs of $15 per unit and variable selling and administrative costs of $6 per unit.

How will the total contribution margin change when output increases from 8,000 to 9,000 units?
questions.solution:
1. CM per unit = $50 − $15 − $6 = $29
  2. Change in units = 9,000 − 8,000 = 1,000
  3. Change in total CM = 1,000 × $29 = increase of $29,000

Both variable costs come out, not just the manufacturing one. Contribution margin is revenue less all variable costs, wherever they sit on the income statement.

questions.stem:
Dugger Company produces shovels. Producing 1,000 shovels costs $3,000 in total. Producing 3,000 shovels costs $7,000 in total.

What is the variable cost per shovel?
questions.solution:
1. Change in cost = $7,000 − $3,000 = $4,000
  2. Change in volume = 3,000 − 1,000 = 2,000
  3. Variable cost = $4,000 / 2,000 = $2.00 per shovel

Option B, $3.00, is $3,000 / 1,000, the average total cost at the low volume. That average mixes fixed cost in, which is exactly what high-low exists to strip out. Fixed cost here is $3,000 − (1,000 × $2.00) = $1,000.

questions.stem:
Peak Industries saw a 20% increase in activity levels over the fourth quarter, within its relevant range.

Which change should the firm expect?
choices: A 20% decrease in variable costs per unit
questions.solution:
Total variable costs rise 20%, because they move in direct proportion to activity.

OptionWhy it fails
Fixed costs up 20%Total fixed cost does not move inside the relevant range.
Total costs up 20%Total cost is variable plus fixed. Only the variable part grows, so total cost rises by less than 20%.
Variable cost per unit down 20%Variable cost per unit is constant. It is fixed cost per unit that falls as volume rises.

questions.stem:
Sailmaster regression output (8 quarters, cost regressed on boats):

Regression Statistics
Multiple R0.955
R Square0.912
Adjusted R Square0.898
Standard Error27,771.27
Observations8
CoefficientsStandard Errort StatP-value
Intercept49,701.2925,332.981.960.0974
Boats687.4387.067.900.0002

t values for 6 degrees of freedom: 70% = 1.134, 80% = 1.440, 90% = 1.943, 95% = 2.447.


What is the interpretation of the p-value on the intercept coefficient?
questions.solution:
His answer, verbatim: 'There is a 9.74 percent chance that the true fixed cost at Sailmaster is 0 (the estimate of $49,701.29 being observed by chance).'

Two things to carry into the exam:

  • He reads a p-value as the probability that the true coefficient is zero, and he wants the threshold at p < 0.05. At 0.0974 the intercept fails that bar, so you cannot be confident Sailmaster has any fixed cost at all.
  • The matching t stat is 1.96, below his rule of thumb of 2. A t below 3 on an intercept means a real chance the cost is entirely variable, in other words that the line runs through the origin.

Compare the Boats row: p = 0.0002 and t = 7.90. The variable cost per boat is solid.

questions.stem:
Sailmaster regression output (8 quarters, cost regressed on boats):

Regression Statistics

Observations8
CoefficientsStandard Errort StatP-value

t values for 6 degrees of freedom: 70% = 1.134, 80% = 1.440, 90% = 1.943, 95% = 2.447.


What is the 90% confidence interval around the fixed cost estimate? Enter the upper bound.
questions.solution:
Fixed cost is the intercept, so use the intercept's own standard error, $25,332.98. Not the 27,771.27 from the top block.

  1. t for 6 df at 90% = 1.943
  2. Half-width = 1.943 × $25,332.98 = $49,221.98
  3. $49,701.29 ± $49,221.98 = ($479.31, $98,923.27)

Read what the interval says. It very nearly includes zero, which is the same story the p-value of 0.0974 told. Wide intervals and weak p-values are two views of one fact.

What is the 80% confidence interval around the variable cost estimate? Enter the upper bound.
questions.solution:
Variable cost is the slope, so use the slope's standard error, $87.06.

  1. t for 6 df at 80% = 1.440
  2. Half-width = 1.440 × $87.06 = $125.3664

Lower confidence, narrower interval. At 80% you need less room than at 95%, so the t multiplier drops from 2.447 to 1.440. Being less confident lets you make a tighter claim.

What is the 95% confidence interval around the total cost estimate at 300 boats? Enter the upper bound.
questions.solution:
This is the one interval that uses the standard error of the regression from the top block, $27,771.27. Coefficient intervals use a coefficient's own standard error; an interval around a predicted cost uses the regression's.

  1. Point estimate = $49,701.29 + (300 × $687.43) = $49,701.29 + $206,229 = $255,930.29

  • He builds the point estimate from the rounded printed coefficients. Use 687.43 and 49,701.29 exactly as shown, not more decimal places from a re-run.

questions.stem:
Cascade Pack sells one trail pack at $72.00. Variable cost is $43.50 per pack and total fixed costs are $219,450.00 per year.

How many packs must Cascade sell to break even? (Round up to the next whole pack.)
questions.solution:
1. $72.00(Volume) − $43.50(Volume) − $219,450.00 = $0
  2. CM per unit = $72.00 − $43.50 = $28.50
  3. $28.50(Volume) = $219,450.00
  4. Volume = $219,450.00 / $28.50 = 7,700.00 → 7,700 packs

Round up. 7,699 packs still loses money.

questions.stem:
Birchwood Services has variable costs equal to 62% of revenue and total fixed costs of $148,800.00.

What annual revenue does Birchwood need to break even?
questions.solution:
No unit price is given, so use the revenue form of the home equation.

  1. Revenue − 0.62(Revenue) − $148,800.00 = $0
  2. 0.38(Revenue) = $148,800.00
  3. Revenue = $148,800.00 / 0.38 = $391,578.95

The CM ratio is 1 − 0.62 = 38%. Divide fixed cost by the CM ratio for a revenue answer, by CM per unit for a unit answer.

questions.stem:
Ridgeline Optics sells a rangefinder for $185.00 with variable cost of $97.00 and annual fixed costs of $341,000.00.

How many rangefinders must it sell to earn $150,000.00 of operating profit before tax? (Round up.)
questions.solution:
1. $185.00(V) − $97.00(V) − $341,000.00 = $150,000.00
  2. $88.00(V) = $341,000.00 + $150,000.00 = $491,000.00
  3. V = 5,579.545 → 5,580 units

Target profit sits next to fixed cost in the numerator. Nothing else about the equation changes.

questions.stem:
Harbor Glass sells a lantern for $45.00. Variable cost is $18.75, annual fixed costs are $262,500.00 and the tax rate is 28%.

How many lanterns must Harbor sell to earn $94,500.00 of after-tax net income? (Round up.)
questions.solution:
1. Gross up first: pretax = $94,500.00 / (1 − 0.28) = $131,250.00
  2. $26.25(V) = $262,500.00 + $131,250.00 = $393,750.00
  3. V = 15,000.000 → 15,000 units

Dividing by (1 − t) makes the target larger. Multiplying by (1 − t) is the single most common error on this question type.

questions.stem:
Tiller Equipment has total assets of $1,250,000.00, financed with $700,000 of debt and $550,000 of equity. Its product sells for $96.00 with variable cost of $54.00, annual fixed costs are $410,000.00 and the tax rate is 25%.

How many units must Tiller sell to earn a 14% after-tax return on assets? (Round up.)
questions.solution:
1. ROA uses total assets: after-tax target = $1,250,000.00 × 14% = $175,000.00
  2. Pretax = $175,000.00 / 0.75 = $233,333.33
  3. $42.00(V) = $410,000.00 + $233,333.33 = $643,333.33
  4. V = 15,317.460 → 15,318 units

Which denominator. ROA uses assets ($1,250,000.00). ROE would use equity ($550,000) and give a different answer. Read the two letters.

questions.stem:
Lakeview Press sells a workbook for $30.00 with variable cost of $12.00. Fixed costs are $108,000.00 and it currently sells 9,500 workbooks.

The owner asks how far sales could fall before the company starts losing money, as a percentage. What is that percentage? (Enter as a number, e.g. 32.5 for 32.5%.)
questions.solution:
1. CM per unit = $18.00, so break-even = $108,000.00 / $18.00 = 6,000 workbooks
  2. Margin of safety = 9,500 − 6,000 = 3,500 workbooks
  3. 'How far can sales fall' divides by current sales: 3,500 / 9,500 = 36.84%

The other denominator. Had he asked 'how far above break-even are we', you would divide by break-even: 3,500 / 6,000 = 58.33%. Same margin of safety, two different percentages. Match the denominator to the words.

questions.stem:
Quarry Tools currently sells 12,000 units at $58.00 with variable cost of $26.00 and fixed costs of $196,000.00.

Next year the price rises 8%, variable cost per unit rises 12% and volume falls 5%. What is next year's operating profit?
questions.solution:
NowNext year
Price$58.00$58.00 × 1.08 = $62.64
Variable cost$26.00$26.00 × 1.12 = $29.12
CM per unit$32.00$33.52
Volume12,00011,400

Fixed cost($196,000.00)($196,000.00)

Rebuild the whole statement. Do not try to adjust the old profit by three percentages: the three changes interact, because CM per unit and volume multiply.

questions.stem:
Summit Pottery expects to sell 7,500 units next year. Variable cost is $31.00 per unit and fixed costs are $288,000.00.

What price must Summit charge to earn $112,500.00 of operating profit?
questions.solution:
1. Price(7,500) − $31.00(7,500) − $288,000.00 = $112,500.00
  2. Price(7,500) = $232,500.00 + $288,000.00 + $112,500.00 = $633,000.00
  3. Price = $633,000.00 / 7,500 = $84.40

Same equation, different unknown. Everything that is not the unknown moves to the right side.

questions.stem:
Fernwood Audio sells 11,000 units at $140.00, with variable cost of $84.00 per unit and fixed costs of $392,000.00.

What is Fernwood's degree of operating leverage? (Round to two decimals.)
questions.solution:
1. Total contribution margin = $56.00 × 11,000 = $616,000.00
  2. Operating profit = $616,000.00 − $392,000.00 = $224,000.00
  3. DOL = $616,000.00 / $224,000.00 = 2.75

Total contribution margin over operating profit. Not CM per unit, not the CM ratio, not revenue.

questions.stem:
Fernwood Audio, same data: 11,000 units at $140.00, variable cost $84.00, fixed costs $392,000.00, DOL = 2.75.

If revenue rises 15%, by what percentage does operating profit rise? (Enter as a number, e.g. 32.5 for 32.5%.)
questions.solution:
1. DOL × %ΔRevenue = %ΔOperating Profit
  2. 2.7500 × 15% = 41.25%

Check it the long way: revenue up 15% means volume 12,649 units, total CM $708,400.00, operating profit $316,400.00. That is 41.25% above $224,000.00. The shortcut and the long way agree.

DOL is a point-in-time number. Once volume moves, DOL itself changes, so do not reuse it for a second step.

Two firms each sell 12,000 units at $200.00.

AlpineBasin
Variable cost per unit$140.00$90.00
Fixed costs$300,000.00$850,000.00

If revenue at both firms falls 20%, what is Basin's new operating profit or loss? (Enter a loss as a negative number.)
questions.solution:
AlpineBasin
CM per unit$60.00$110.00
Total CM at 12,000$720,000.00$1,320,000.00
Operating profit$420,000.00$470,000.00
DOL1.712.81
Break-even units5,0007,728
Profit after a 20% drop$276,000.00$206,000.00

Basin: $110.00 × 9,600 = $1,056,000.00, less $850,000.00 = $206,000.00.

What operating leverage means. Both firms earn identical profit at 12,000 units. Basin carries the higher fixed base, so its DOL is 2.81 against Alpine's 1.71. The same 20% revenue fall costs Basin 56.2% of profit and Alpine 34.3%. High leverage pays more on the way up and hurts more on the way down.

Check with DOL: 2.8085 × −20% = -56.17% of $470,000.00 = $-264,000.00 change, landing at $206,000.00. ✓

questions.stem:
Granite Supply sells two models in a constant mix.

StandardDeluxe
Price$40.00$65.00
Variable cost$22.00$31.00
Expected unit sales9,0003,000

Total fixed costs are $455,000.00. How many Standard units are needed to break even? (Round up.)
questions.solution:
Basket method.

  1. Unit mix = 9,000 : 3,000 = 3 : 1
  2. Basket price = 3($40.00) + 1($65.00) = $185.00
  3. Basket variable cost = 3($22.00) + 1($31.00) = $97.00
  4. Basket CM = $88.00
  5. Baskets = $455,000.00 / $88.00 = 5,170.4545
  6. Unpack before rounding: Standard = 5,170.4545 × 3 = 15,511.3636 → 15,512; Deluxe = 5,170.4545 → 5,171

Total = 20,683 units. Unpack first, then round each product up. Rounding the basket count first throws the unit answers off by up to one basket's worth of each product.

questions.stem:
Granite Supply, same data: Standard $40.00 price / $22.00 variable cost / 9,000 units; Deluxe $65.00 / $31.00 / 3,000 units; fixed costs $455,000.00.

What is the break-even point in total revenue?
questions.solution:
A dollar answer calls for the revenue method.

ProductRevenueVariable cost
Standard$360,000.00$198,000.00
Deluxe$195,000.00$93,000.00
Total$555,000.00$291,000.00
  1. Variable cost ratio = $291,000.00 / $555,000.00 = 0.524324
  2. Revenue − 0.524324(Revenue) = $455,000.00
  3. Revenue = $455,000.00 / 0.475676 = $956,534.09

Cross-check against the basket answer: 15,512 Standard × $40.00 + 5,171 Deluxe × $65.00 = $956,595.00. The small gap is the rounding-up of each product. Both methods are correct.

questions.stem:
Granite Supply, same data (Standard $40.00/$22.00, Deluxe $65.00/$31.00, mix 3 : 1, fixed costs $455,000.00).

Using the weighted-average contribution margin per unit method, what is the weighted-average CM per unit?
questions.solution:
1. Unit-volume weights: Standard 3/4 = 75%, Deluxe 1/4 = 25%
  2. CM per unit: Standard $18.00, Deluxe $34.00
  3. Weighted average = 0.75($18.00) + 0.25($34.00) = $13.50 + $8.50 = $22.00

Then total break-even units = $455,000.00 / $22.00 = 20,681.82 → 20,682 units, split 75/25.

Weight by unit volume, not by revenue. Revenue weights belong to the CM-ratio method. Mixing the two is the classic error here. All three methods (basket, weighted average, revenue) give the same economics; they differ only in what the answer is expressed in.

questions.stem:
Kestrel Labs sells three kits in a constant mix.

CorePlusPro
Price$25.00$48.00$90.00
Variable cost$11.00$23.00$52.00
Expected units20,00012,0004,000

Fixed costs are $612,000.00. How many Pro kits must Kestrel sell to earn $200,000.00 of operating profit? (Round up.)
questions.solution:
1. Unit mix = 20,000 : 12,000 : 4,000 = 5 : 3 : 1
  2. Basket price = 5($25.00) + 3($48.00) + 1($90.00) = $359.00
  3. Basket variable cost = 5($11.00) + 3($23.00) + 1($52.00) = $176.00
  4. Basket CM = $183.00
  5. Baskets = ($612,000.00 + $200,000.00) / $183.00 = 4,437.1585
  6. Core 22,185.79 → 22,186; Plus 13,311.48 → 13,312; Pro 4,437.16 → 4,438

The greatest common divisor of the three volumes is 4,000, which gives the smallest whole-number basket. Any proportional basket works; smaller numbers just keep the arithmetic clean.

questions.stem:
Kestrel Labs, same prices and costs (Core $25.00/$11.00, Plus $48.00/$23.00, Pro $90.00/$52.00), fixed costs $612,000.00.

Marketing shifts the mix to equal unit volumes of the three kits. What is the new total break-even volume in units? (Round each product up, then total.)
questions.solution:
1. New mix = 1 : 1 : 1, so use a 3-unit basket of 1 each (or 3 : 3 : 3)
  2. Basket price = $163.00; basket variable cost = $86.00; basket CM = $77.00 per 3 units
  3. Baskets = $612,000.00 / $231.00 = 2,649.3506
  4. Each product = 7,948.05 → 7,949 units, so total = 23,847 units

Compare. Under the original 5 : 3 : 1 mix, break-even was 30,100 units. Under 1 : 1 : 1 it is 23,847. Fewer units are needed because the mix moved toward Pro, whose CM per unit ($38.00) is the highest. This is why there is no single multi-product break-even: every answer is conditional on a mix assumption.

questions.stem:
Westbrook Mill tracked maintenance cost against machine hours.

MonthMachine hoursMaintenance cost
January1,200$48,000.00
February2,050$62,350.00
March1,460$52,900.00
April2,600$70,400.00
May1,880$58,100.00
June2,310$66,250.00

Using the high-low method, what is the variable cost per machine hour (the b term)? Round to the nearest cent.
questions.solution:
1. Pick high and low by machine hours, the activity driver: high = April (2,600 hours, $70,400.00); low = January (1,200 hours, $48,000.00)
  2. b = ($70,400.00 − $48,000.00) / (2,600 − 1,200) = $22,400.00 / 1,400 = $16.00 per hour

Here the highest hours and the highest cost happen to be the same month, which is not guaranteed. Always sort on the driver anyway, so the habit holds when they diverge.

questions.stem:
Westbrook Mill, same data (high April: 2,600 hours, $70,400.00; low January: 1,200 hours, $48,000.00; b = $16.00).

What is total fixed maintenance cost per month (the a term)?
questions.solution:
1. a = High cost − b(High activity) = $70,400.00 − $16.00(2,600) = $70,400.00 − $41,600.00 = $28,800.00
  2. Check at the low point: $48,000.00 − $16.00(1,200) = $28,800.00 ✓

The cost function is TC = $16.00(Hours) + $28,800.00. Always run the check at the other point; if the two intercepts differ by more than rounding, the slope is wrong.

questions.stem:
Westbrook Mill's cost function from high-low is TC = $16.00(Machine hours) + $28,800.00.

What is the predicted total maintenance cost at 2,000 machine hours?
questions.solution:
1. TC = $16.00(2,000) + $28,800.00
  2. = $32,000.00 + $28,800.00 = $60,800.00

2,000 hours sits inside the observed range of 1,200 to 2,600, so this is interpolation and the estimate is defensible. Predicting at 6,000 hours would be outside the relevant range, where the linear cost function stops being trustworthy.

questions.stem:
Hollis Courier recorded delivery cost against number of deliveries.

WeekDeliveriesDelivery cost
Week 1420$9,180.00
Week 2610$11,300.00
Week 3370$8,900.00
Week 4580$11,560.00
Week 5505$10,100.00

Using the high-low method, what is the variable cost per delivery? Round to the nearest cent.
questions.solution:
Watch the rows. Week 4 has the highest cost ($11,560.00) but Week 2 has the most deliveries (610). High-low sorts on the driver, so use Week 2 and Week 3.

  1. b = ($11,300.00 − $8,900.00) / (610 − 370) = $2,400.00 / 240 = $10.00
  2. a = $11,300.00 − $10.00(610) = $5,200.00

Sorting by cost instead would pair Week 4 with Week 3 and give $12.67 per delivery, which is wrong.

questions.stem:
Northgate Casting reports that at 18,000 units, cost per unit is $26.00 variable plus $30.00 fixed, for a total of $56.00 per unit.

What is total cost if volume rises to 24,000 units, still inside the relevant range?
questions.solution:
1. Recover total fixed cost: $30.00 × 18,000 = $540,000.00
  2. Total cost = $26.00(24,000) + $540,000.00 = $624,000.00 + $540,000.00 = $1,164,000.00

The trap, and it is on his slides with a red NO. Multiplying the $56.00 total cost per unit by 24,000 gives $1,344,000.00, overstating cost by $180,000.00. Fixed cost per unit is only valid at the volume where it was computed. At 24,000 units the fixed cost per unit falls to $22.50.

Never unitize fixed cost. Never unitize profit either.

questions.stem:
Pinemark Furniture sold 16,000 chairs last quarter. Its GAAP income statement:

Sales revenue$960,000.00
Cost of goods sold($624,000.00)
Gross margin$336,000.00
Selling and administrative($186,000.00)
Operating income$150,000.00

Per chair: direct materials $14.00, direct labor $9.00, variable overhead $5.00, variable selling $3.00. All other costs are fixed.

What are total fixed costs for the quarter?
questions.solution:
A GAAP statement splits core versus run the business. CVP needs variable versus fixed. Those are different cuts, so rebuild the split.

  1. Variable cost per chair = $14.00 + $9.00 + $5.00 + $3.00 = $31.00
  2. Total variable cost = $31.00 × 16,000 = $496,000.00
  3. Total cost = $624,000.00 + $186,000.00 = $810,000.00
  4. Total fixed cost = $810,000.00 − $496,000.00 = $314,000.00

Cost of goods sold is not the variable cost and selling and admin is not the fixed cost. Both lines mix the two. Price is $60.00 per chair, so CM per chair is $29.00 and break-even is 10,828 chairs.

questions.stem:
Rowan Clinic pays each nurse $6,200 per month and one nurse can handle up to 400 patient visits per month. Other fixed costs are $31,000 per month and variable supplies cost $14 per visit.

What is total monthly cost at 1,050 visits?
questions.solution:
1. Nurses needed = 1,050 / 400 = 2.625 → 3 nurses (you cannot hire 0.625 of a nurse)
  2. Nurse cost = 3 × $6,200 = $18,600.00
  3. Other fixed = $31,000.00
  4. Variable supplies = $14 × 1,050 = $14,700.00
  5. Total = $64,300.00

Step cost. Nurse salary is fixed within a 400-visit band and jumps at each boundary. Treating it as variable at $6,200/400 = $15.50 per visit gives $61,975.00, which understates cost because the third nurse is only two-thirds used. The relevant range here is 801 to 1,200 visits.

questions.stem:
Ellis Tooling reports revenue of $1,480,000, total variable costs of $917,600 and total fixed costs of $402,000.

What is Ellis's contribution margin ratio? (Enter as a number, e.g. 32.5 for 32.5%.)
questions.solution:
1. Total contribution margin = $1,480,000 − $917,600 = $562,400.00
  2. CM ratio = $562,400.00 / $1,480,000 = 38.00%

Fixed cost never enters a CM ratio. The variable cost ratio is the complement: 62.00%, and the two sum to 100%.

Operating profit is $160,400.00, break-even revenue is $402,000 / 0.380000 = $1,057,894.74, and DOL is $562,400.00 / $160,400.00 = 3.51.

Larkspur Distribution wants its shipping cost split into variable and fixed components.

QuarterUnits shippedShipping cost
Q13,400$171,000.00
Q24,900$199,500.00
Q32,800$159,600.00
Q45,600$212,800.00

Using the high-low method, what is total fixed shipping cost per quarter?

A classmate says: "Our fixed costs are $600,000 and we make 40,000 units, so our fixed cost is $15 per unit. At 50,000 units our total cost will be 50,000 times the $15 plus the variable cost."

In three or four sentences, explain what is wrong with this reasoning and state the correct way to compute total cost at 50,000 units.
questions.solution:
What is wrong: fixed cost per unit is only valid at the volume where it was computed. Total fixed cost stays at $600,000 across the relevant range, so spreading it over 50,000 units gives $12 per unit, not $15. Multiplying the $15 by 50,000 counts $150,000 of fixed cost that does not exist.

The correct method: never unitize fixed cost. Use

Total Cost = VC Rate (Volume) + Total Fixed Cost

So total cost at 50,000 units is (variable rate × 50,000) + $600,000.

Marking. Credit lands on three things: fixed cost in total does not change with volume; fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises; and the total-cost equation keeps fixed cost as a lump. If you only say 'he should not unitize', you have stated the rule without the reason.

questions.stem:
Ardmore Cabinetry sold 24,000 cabinets last year at $62.00 each.

Sales revenue$1,488,000.00
Cost of goods sold($1,018,000.00)
Gross margin$470,000.00
Selling and administrative($274,000.00)
Operating income$196,000.00

Per cabinet: direct materials $17.00, direct labor $11.50, variable overhead $4.00, variable selling $2.50. Every other cost is fixed.

What are Ardmore's total fixed costs for the year?
questions.solution:
The statement is cut into core versus run-the-business. CVP needs variable versus fixed. Rebuild it.

  1. Variable cost per cabinet = $17.00 + $11.50 + $4.00 + $2.50 = $35.00
  2. Total variable cost = $35.00 × 24,000 = $840,000.00
  3. Total cost = $1,018,000.00 + $274,000.00 = $1,292,000.00
  4. Total fixed cost = $1,292,000.00 − $840,000.00 = $452,000.00

Cost of goods sold is not the variable cost; selling and admin is not the fixed cost. Both lines are mixtures.

questions.stem:
Bellweather Services regressed total service-department cost on the number of service calls for the last eight quarters. The Excel Regression output:

Regression Statistics
Multiple R0.9842
R Square0.9686
Adjusted R Square0.9633
Standard Error10,500.02
Observations8
CoefficientsStandard Errort StatP-value
Intercept30,000.2914,993.942.000.0923
Service calls85.006.2513.600.0000

t values for 6 degrees of freedom: 70% = 1.134, 80% = 1.440, 90% = 1.943, 95% = 2.447.

Build a 90% confidence interval around the estimate of variable cost per service call. Enter the upper bound.
questions.solution:
Variable cost is the slope, so use the slope's own standard error, 6.25. Not the 10,500.02 from the top block and not the intercept's 14,993.94.

  1. t for 6 df at 90% = 1.943
  2. Half-width = 1.943 × 6.25 = $12.14
  3. $85.00 ± $12.14 = ($72.86, $97.14)

Degrees of freedom = n − 2 = 8 − 2 = 6. One estimated coefficient plus one intercept, so you lose two.

Bellweather expects 2,800 service calls next quarter. Estimate total service-department cost and build a 95% confidence interval around that estimate. Enter the upper bound.
questions.solution:
This is the one interval that uses the standard error of the regression from the top block, 10,500.02. A coefficient's interval uses that coefficient's standard error; an interval around a predicted cost uses the regression's.

  1. Point estimate = $30,000.29 + $85.00(2,800) = $30,000.29 + $238,000.00 = $268,000.29
  2. Half-width = 2.447 × 10,500.02 = $25,693.55

Two habits that earn the marks: compute the point estimate first, and build it from the printed rounded coefficients exactly as shown.

Worth noticing: the intercept's p-value is 0.0923 and its t stat is 2.00. By his thresholds (t of 2 is useful, over 3 is essentially certain, p under 0.05) the fixed cost is only marginally supported. The variable cost per call, at t = 13.60, is solid.

questions.stem:
Coldbrook Brewing sells one keg system at $128.00. Variable cost is $71.00 per system and annual fixed costs are $621,300.00.

How many systems must Coldbrook sell to break even?
questions.solution:
1. $128.00(V) − $71.00(V) − $621,300.00 = $0
  2. CM per unit = $57.00
  3. V = $621,300.00 / $57.00 = 10,900.0000 → 10,900 systems

Round up. Break-even always rounds up.

questions.stem:
Coldbrook Brewing, same data: price $128.00, variable cost $71.00, fixed costs $621,300.00. Its tax rate is 26%.

How many systems must Coldbrook sell to earn $210,000.00 of after-tax net income?
questions.solution:
1. Gross up to pretax: $210,000.00 / (1 − 0.26) = $283,783.78
  2. $57.00(V) = $621,300.00 + $283,783.78 = $905,083.78
  3. V = 15,878.6629 → 15,879 systems

Divide by (1 − t). The pretax target must be larger than the after-tax target, never smaller.

questions.stem:
Coldbrook Brewing, same data: price $128.00, variable cost $71.00, fixed costs $621,300.00. It currently sells 14,000 systems a year.

The owner wants to know how far above the break-even point current sales are, as a percentage. Report that percentage. (Enter as a number, e.g. 32.5 for 32.5%.)
questions.solution:
1. Break-even = 10,900 systems (from item 7)
  2. Margin of safety = 14,000 − 10,900 = 3,100 systems
  3. 'How far above break-even' divides by break-even: 3,100 / 10,900 = 28.44%

The denominator is the whole question. Dividing by current sales gives 3,100 / 14,000 = 22.14%, which answers a different question: how far sales could fall. Read the words and pick the denominator to match.

Ironwood Gear sells two pack models in a constant sales mix. Total fixed costs are $1,045,000.00.

TrailSummit
Selling price$85.00$140.00
Variable cost$49.00$76.00
Expected unit sales16,0006,000

How many Summit packs must Ironwood sell to break even?
questions.solution:
Basket method.

  1. Unit mix = 16,000 : 6,000 = 8 : 3
  2. Basket price = 8($85.00) + 3($140.00) = $1,100.00
  3. Basket variable cost = 8($49.00) + 3($76.00) = $620.00
  4. Basket CM = $480.00
  5. Baskets = $1,045,000.00 / $480.00 = 2,177.0833
  6. Unpack before rounding: Trail = 2,177.0833 × 8 = 17,416.6667 → 17,417; Summit = 2,177.0833 × 3 = 6,531.2500 → 6,532

Total 23,949 packs. Reducing the mix by its common divisor keeps the arithmetic clean; any proportional basket gives the same unpacked answer.

questions.stem:
Ironwood Gear, same data (Trail $85.00 / $49.00 / 16,000 units; Summit $140.00 / $76.00 / 6,000 units; fixed costs $1,045,000.00).

What total sales revenue does Ironwood need to earn $320,000.00 of operating profit?
questions.solution:
A revenue answer calls for the revenue method: build the overall variable cost ratio.

ProductRevenueVariable cost
Trail$1,360,000.00$784,000.00
Summit$840,000.00$456,000.00
Total$2,200,000.00$1,240,000.00
  1. Variable cost ratio = $1,240,000.00 / $2,200,000.00 = 0.563636
  2. CM ratio = 0.436364
  3. Revenue − 0.563636(Revenue) − $1,045,000.00 = $320,000.00
  4. Revenue = ($1,045,000.00 + $320,000.00) / 0.436364 = $3,128,125.00

Revenue weights, not unit weights. The unit mix is 8 : 3 but the revenue mix is 61.82% / 38.18%, because Summit carries the higher price.

questions.stem:
Marlow Instruments sells 19,000 units at $96.00, with variable cost of $52.00 per unit and fixed costs of $528,000.00.

What is Marlow's degree of operating leverage? (Round to two decimals.)
questions.solution:
1. Total contribution margin = $44.00 × 19,000 = $836,000.00
  2. Operating profit = $836,000.00 − $528,000.00 = $308,000.00
  3. DOL = $836,000.00 / $308,000.00 = 2.71

Total contribution margin over operating profit. A 10% revenue rise would lift operating profit 27.14%.

questions.stem:
Two competitors sell the same product at the same price and currently earn identical operating profit at identical volume. Firm X leases its equipment and pays a per-unit royalty; Firm Y bought its equipment outright and pays no royalty.

In three or four sentences, explain which firm has the higher operating leverage, what that means for each firm if industry demand falls 25%, and why the two firms can have different degrees of operating leverage while earning the same profit today.
questions.solution:
Firm Y has the higher operating leverage. Buying the equipment converts what Firm X pays per unit into a fixed cost, so Y has a larger fixed base and a higher contribution margin per unit.

If demand falls 25%: Y loses far more profit. Y's contribution margin per unit is larger, so each lost unit costs it more, and its fixed costs do not shrink with volume. Y's break-even is higher and its margin of safety smaller. X's costs fall away with its volume, cushioning the drop.

Why identical profit but different leverage: operating leverage is about the shape of the cost structure, not its level. The two firms sit at the same point today; they differ in the slope of profit as volume moves away from that point.

Marking. Name Y, tie it to the fixed-for-variable swap, and say the consequence runs both ways: Y gains more on a 25% rise too. Credit also for distinguishing operating leverage, a stable characteristic of the cost structure, from DOL, which is a point-in-time sensitivity that changes as soon as volume moves.

questions.stem:
Falconridge Aerospace builds one aircraft model. All figures are in millions of dollars. This year it produced 9 aircraft and sold 7 at $112.00 million each. There was no beginning inventory.

CostAmountBehavior
Direct materials$31.00 per aircraftvariable, manufacturing
Direct labor$18.00 per aircraftvariable, manufacturing
Variable overhead$9.00 per aircraftvariable, manufacturing
Fixed manufacturing overhead$144.00 totalfixed, manufacturing
Selling and administrative$86.00 totalfixed, period cost

Compute Falconridge's operating profit for the year, in millions.
questions.solution:
Manufacturing costs attach to the aircraft and follow them. Only the 7 sold reach the income statement. Selling and admin is a period cost and is expensed in full.

  1. Variable manufacturing cost per aircraft = $31.00 + $18.00 + $9.00 = $58.00
  2. Total manufacturing cost = ($58.00 × 9) + $144.00 = $522.00 + $144.00 = $666.00
  3. Cost per aircraft = $666.00 / 9 = $74.0000
  4. Cost of goods sold = $74.0000 × 7 = $518.00
Revenue ($112.00 × 7)$784.00
Cost of goods sold($518.00)
Gross margin$266.00
Selling and administrative($86.00)
Operating profit$180.00

The trap. Expensing all $144.00 of fixed manufacturing overhead this year understates profit, because $32.00 of it sits in the 2 unsold aircraft. Divide the fixed overhead across everything produced, not everything sold.

Compute the value of Falconridge's ending finished-goods inventory, in millions.
questions.solution:
1. Cost per aircraft = $666.00 / 9 = $74.0000
  2. Unsold aircraft = 9 − 7 = 2
  3. Ending inventory = $74.0000 × 2 = $148.00

Check that it ties: total manufacturing cost $666.00 = cost of goods sold $518.00 + ending inventory $148.00. ✓

Inventory carries its share of fixed manufacturing overhead as well as the variable cost. Valuing it at the $58.00 variable cost alone gives $116.00 and understates it by $32.00. Selling and admin never enters inventory.

questions.stem:
Beacon Clinic staffs one technician per shift. Each technician costs $7,400.00 per month and can handle up to 500 patient visits a month. Other fixed costs are $46,000.00 a month and variable supplies cost $19.00 per visit.

What is Beacon's total cost in a month with 1,640 visits?
questions.solution:
1. Technicians needed = 1,640 / 500 = 3.28 → 4 technicians (you cannot staff a fraction of one)
  2. Technician cost = 4 × $7,400.00 = $29,600.00
  3. Other fixed = $46,000.00
  4. Variable supplies = $19.00 × 1,640 = $31,160.00
  5. Total = $106,760.00

Step cost. Technician pay is fixed inside a 500-visit band and jumps at each boundary. Treating it as variable at $14.80 per visit gives $101,432.00, which understates cost because the 4th technician is only 28% used. The relevant range here is 1,501 to 2,000 visits.

From class discussion only. Every fact in this item comes from the recorded class session named below. No case document, question sheet or Excel template was opened to build it, and nothing here is derived from one.

In class he compared Giulia's two futures. Today she outsources: $11.00 price, $10.45 variable cost, no fixed cost at all, 1,000 units a month, and so an operating income of $550 and a break even of zero. If she signs with Stanley and takes on the forge, her cost structure changes completely, and at 4,000 units the labor-variable and labor-fixed treatments both land on roughly the same operating income.

In 50 words or fewer, tell Giulia what she is actually choosing between. Name what the outsourced structure costs her as well as what it protects, and name what the forge exposes her to. Do not recompute anything.
questions.solution:
A 49-word answer that would earn the marks:

She is choosing a cost structure, not a profit. Outsourcing has no fixed cost: she cannot lose, breaks even at zero, but is capped near $550. The forge adds fixed cost and leverage: far more upside per unit, real losses below break even. It turns on her volume confidence.

That is 49 words. Count them before you submit.

What the class actually landed on. He put the outsourced world up first and called it safe: revenue minus variable cost of $0.55 a unit, zero fixed cost, so break even is zero units and nothing can go wrong. His own words on the result were that $550 is "not all that inspiring, right? Safe, but not all that inspiring". That pairing, safe and uninspiring, is the whole point of the item.

The three things worth 10 points here.

  1. No fixed cost means no break even and no downside. It also means no leverage, so the upside is capped at $0.55 a unit however well she sells.
  2. Taking the forge converts that into a fixed-cost structure. He said of the outsourced position: "No leverage, no risk, and therefore sort of very little upside down."
  3. So the decision is a judgement about volume confidence, not about which option shows the better number at one volume. At 4,000 units the two treatments of labor look almost identical and behave nothing alike the moment volume moves.

Under 50 words, say the thing and stop. No preamble, no restating the facts he gave you, no "in my opinion". One clause per idea.

cite.quote: Safe, but not all that inspiring

cite2.quote: No leverage, no risk, and therefore sort of very little upside down.
