From class discussion only. Every fact in this item comes from the recorded class session named below. No case document, question sheet or Excel template was opened to build it, and nothing here is derived from one.

In class he worked the hammer line two ways. Incrementally, hammers add $7,064 of monthly operating income and show a gross margin of 35%. Then he applied Giulia's own estimate of productive labor time to allocate the costs other than materials, and the same hammer line showed a gross margin of 3%.

In 90 words or fewer, answer the question he put to the room: should the 3% change the decision to add hammers? Say what the allocation does and does not change, say why she must still care about the 3%, and name the view you would decide on.
questions.solution:
A 77-word answer that would earn the marks:

No. The allocation moves reported margin between lines; it changes no cash flow and no incremental profit. The decision question is whether hammers add, and incrementally they add $7,064 a month at a 35% margin, so the answer stands. But she must still care about the 3%, because that is how the line will appear to outsiders: lenders, buyers and investors read allocated, GAAP-style statements. Decide on the incremental view; manage the appearance of the allocated one.

That is 77 words. Count them before you submit.

This is his own structure, almost his words. He asked the room directly whether the very different appearance "should have implications for the decision? Should I add Hammers?" and answered it himself: "Maybe, maybe. You have to care about performance but also appearance." Then he closed the loop: it "doesn't mean she shouldn't do it. But it does mean, yes, she needs to care about this, even if this seems sort of wacky to us."

The four things worth 10 points here.

  1. Allocation redistributes; it creates and destroys nothing. Total firm profit is identical either way.
  2. The decision question is incremental, so it is answered on the incremental numbers.
  3. Appearance is still real. Performance and appearance are two different things she has to manage, and he said so in those words.
  4. Saying "the allocation is arbitrary so ignore it" is the trap. He never says ignore it.

Watch the allocation percentage. In the same session he says 37% of productive labor time goes to hammers and later says 63% goes to hammers and 37% to pitons. Both are on the recording. If a question hands you one of them, use the one you are handed and do not reconcile them.

questions.stem: Firm A and Firm B sell the same product at the same price, sell the same number of units, and report the same operating profit this year. Firm A's costs are mostly fixed; Firm B's are mostly variable. In two or three sentences, say which firm has the higher degree of operating leverage and what that means for next year's profit if revenue falls 10 percent.
questions.solution:
Firm A. Same profit on same revenue means the two firms have the same Revenue minus Variable Cost minus Fixed Cost; but Firm A gets there with a large Total FC and a low VC Rate, so its total contribution margin is larger.

DOL = Total contribution margin / Operating profit. Same denominator, larger numerator, so Firm A's DOL is higher.

DOL x %change in Revenue = %change in Operating Profit. A 10 percent revenue fall costs Firm A a larger percentage of profit than Firm B. Leverage cuts both ways: the same structure that magnifies a gain magnifies a loss.

Full marks need all three: names Firm A, names the cost structure as the reason, and states the direction of the profit effect.

questions.stem: A classmate writes: "Our DOL is 3.2, so our DOL will still be 3.2 next year." In two or three sentences, say what is wrong with that and what does stay the same.
questions.solution:
DOL is a point-in-time number, not a property of the firm. It is computed at one volume: Total contribution margin / Operating profit, both measured at that volume.

As volume rises, contribution margin and operating profit both rise, but fixed cost does not, so operating profit rises faster and the ratio falls. Move away from break even and DOL shrinks toward 1. Move toward break even and DOL grows without limit, because the denominator goes to zero.

What stays the same is the operating leverage itself: the cost structure, the split between Total FC and VC Rate. That is a characteristic of how the firm is built. DOL is this year's reading off that structure.

Full marks need the point-in-time / structure distinction, plus the direction DOL moves as volume rises.

questions.stem: A manufacturer is choosing between leasing equipment for a flat $400,000 per year and paying a contractor $14 per unit for the same work. Volume next year is uncertain. In two or three sentences, state the trade-off in terms of operating leverage and name the volume at which the two options cost the same.
questions.solution:
Indifference volume: 400,000 = 14(Volume), so Volume = 28,571.43, which rounds to 28,572 units before the lease is cheaper.

The lease converts variable cost into fixed cost. It raises Total FC, lowers the VC Rate, and so raises contribution margin per unit and the degree of operating leverage. Above 28,572 units the lease is cheaper and profit climbs faster per extra unit. Below it the contractor is cheaper and the firm is less exposed if volume disappoints.

Note the shape of the answer: higher leverage is not better or worse on its own. It is a bet on volume.

Full marks need the indifference volume, the direction the lease moves leverage, and the statement that the choice depends on expected volume.

questions.stem: Two divisions report the same revenue. Division One has DOL of 1.4; Division Two has DOL of 6.0. In two or three sentences, say what that tells you about each division's position relative to its break-even point, and what it does not tell you.
questions.solution:
DOL = Total contribution margin / Operating profit. A DOL of 6.0 means operating profit is only one sixth of contribution margin, so fixed cost is eating five sixths of it: Division Two is close to its break-even point. A DOL of 1.4 means fixed cost is small against contribution margin, so Division One is well clear of break even.

What it does not tell you: the level of profit. DOL is a ratio. Division Two could be the larger earner in dollars and still carry the higher DOL, if its fixed costs are large. DOL answers how sensitive profit is, never how big it is.

Full marks need the relationship to break even in both directions, plus the point that DOL says nothing about the level of profit.
